Both labels are valid in their own domain; do NOT sneer at 'vegetable' — the point is the two words answer different questions (kitchen use vs botany). The Nix v. Hedden rung is food-anchored (the tomato and its tariff are the subject, not the court). Dinner-test payoff = the strawberry-isn't-a-berry rung. Keep the seed-carrying clue OUT of the stem so all four choices stay live.

topics.name: The onion family: bulbs and tears (alliums)
topics.strand: What part of the plant we eat
topics.scope: Onions and garlic are BULBS — underground storage buds wrapped in swollen leaves — and their whole personality (the layers, the tears, the sweet-when-cooked magic) comes from sulfur chemistry the plant built to fend off pests. T1: an onion is a BULB — a short squat stem ringed by fat overlapping storage leaves; every ring you slice is one of those leaves, and the papery skin is the outermost, dried one. T2 (dinner-test payoff, mechanism): cutting an onion ruptures its cells and mixes chemicals into a stinging sulfur gas that drifts up and irritates your eyes — chilling the onion or cutting it under water slows the sting. T3: garlic is a bulb split into cloves, and each clove is itself a little storage bud that can grow a whole new plant; garlic's sharp smell only appears once you crush or cut it and release its sulfur compound. T4: cooking transforms the alliums — heat turns those harsh sulfur compounds into sweet ones, which is why raw garlic bites but roasted garlic goes mild, brown and jammy (a cousin of the browning that sweetens fried onions).
topics.source: Onion/garlic = bulbs of concentric swollen leaf bases; lachrymatory sulfur gas released on cutting; garlic's aroma forms only when crushed; sulfur chemistry mellows with heat: settled culinary/food-science fact. Grokipedia attempted first (HTTP 403); corroborate at build via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Onion, /Garlic, /Syn-Propanethial-S-oxide.
topics.framing_note: Lead with the phenomenon ('why does chopping an onion sting your eyes?'), never 'What is a bulb?'. The mechanism answer stays food-level ('a sulfur gas'), NOT the enzyme/compound Latin name (that name is banned as the tested answer; it may be a distractor). Dinner-test payoff = the tears rung. Keep 'each ring is a leaf' as the T1 wonder.

topics.name: The peanut that buries itself (a legume, not a nut)
topics.strand: What part of the plant we eat
topics.scope: The peanut breaks every 'nut' rule — it is a bean that flowers in the air then plants its own pods underground, and that legume identity rewrote Southern farming. T1: a peanut is not a nut — it is a LEGUME, a member of the bean and pea family, and it grows inside a pod like other beans. T2 (dinner-test payoff, the amazing fact): the peanut flowers ABOVE ground, then a stalk from the spent flower bends down and pushes the developing pod DOWN INTO the soil, where the peanuts ripen underground (a trick called geocarpy). T3: because it is a legume, the peanut plant hosts bacteria that pull nitrogen out of the air and enrich the soil, so planting peanuts helps refill land that other crops drain. T4 (food-history): George Washington Carver urged Southern farmers to rotate soil-exhausting cotton with peanuts to rebuild worn-out land, then promoted dozens of peanut uses so farmers would have a market for the harvest.
topics.source: Verified: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peanut (legume in Fabaceae, not a true nut; geocarpy via the peg/gynophore burying the pod; nitrogen-fixing; Carver promoted it as a soil-restoring rotation crop after cotton). Grokipedia attempted first (HTTP 403).
topics.framing_note: Lead with the paradox/scene ('a peanut plant flowers in the air — so where do the peanuts form?'), never 'What is a legume?'. Accuracy rails: peanut = legume (bean family), NOT a botanical nut; Carver promoted it as a rotation crop and popularizer of uses — he did NOT invent peanut butter, don't imply it. Dinner-test payoff = the geocarpy/buries-itself rung. Keep the answer food-anchored (the peanut/pod/soil), not the bare term 'geocarpy'.

topics.name: The potato: a stem that grew underground (tubers)
topics.strand: What part of the plant we eat
topics.scope: A potato is not a root — it is a swollen underground STEM (a tuber) the plant packs with starch, and that identity explains its eyes, its poison, and its history. T1: a potato is a TUBER — a swollen underground stem, not a root; the 'eyes' are buds, and a chunk with an eye will sprout a whole new plant, which is why potatoes are grown from potatoes, not seeds. T2 (origin): the potato is Andean — domesticated thousands of years ago high in the mountains of Peru and Bolivia near Lake Titicaca, long before it reached Europe. T3 (same-name surprise): a sweet potato is NOT a potato — it is a storage ROOT of a different plant (a morning-glory relative), while the true potato is a stem; same name, different organ, different family. T4 (honest safety): a green or heavily sprouted potato is building up solanine, a natural toxin (the potato is in the nightshade family), so the green tinge under the skin is a warning to cut it away. T5a (food-history): after 1492 the Columbian Exchange carried the potato to Europe, where its huge calories-per-acre helped populations and armies boom. T5b (dinner-test payoff): the Irish Great Famine (1845) hit so hard because the poor lived on one cloned variety (the 'Lumper') with no genetic variety — so when the blight Phytophthora infestans arrived, the whole crop rotted at once (a monoculture catastrophe).
topics.source: Verified: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potato (stem tuber not root; eyes are buds; Andes near Lake Titicaca ~7,000-10,000 yrs; Solanaceae/solanine in green potatoes; Columbian Exchange; 1845 Great Famine, Phytophthora infestans, Lumper). Sweet-potato-is-a-root/Convolvulaceae: settled botany. Grokipedia attempted first (HTTP 403).
topics.framing_note: Scene-first ('dig one up — why does it grow eyes?'), never 'What is a tuber?'. Accuracy rails: potato = Andean (never Irish/European in origin); tuber = STEM not root; sweet potato is a different plant and a root. The famine rung is food-anchored (the blight and the monoculture crop are the subject, not British policy) and is the dinner-test payoff. Keep the solanine rung matter-of-fact, not scary.

topics.name: Chowder and the tomato feud
topics.scope: A soup named for a pot, and the war over its color. T1: 'chowder' is named after the POT, not an ingredient — from the French 'chaudiere,' the big iron cauldron that French and Breton fishermen boiled their catch in on the docks; the earliest chowders had no clams and no milk, just ship's biscuit, salt pork, and fish. T2: NEW ENGLAND clam chowder is the CREAMY WHITE one — milk or cream, potatoes, onion, clams — and its flavor base starts by rendering SALT PORK and softening onion in that fat. T3: MANHATTAN clam chowder is the RED, TOMATO-based one with NO cream — an offense so grave that New Englanders called it a 'notable heresy'; this is the heart of the feud. T4: the feud reached the LAW — in 1939 a Maine legislator introduced a bill to make putting TOMATOES in clam chowder ILLEGAL; it failed, but the rivalry stuck. (Rhode Island even has a clear-broth chowder with neither cream nor tomato.)
topics.source: Wikipedia 'Chowder'; Atlas Obscura 'Chowder Once Had No Milk...'; etymology (French chaudiere from Latin calidus); 1939 Maine anti-tomato bill (Rep. Cleveland Sleeper, Rockland).
topics.framing_note: Scene-led, never 'What is chowder?'. INVERT THE WONDER on the name: chowder is named after the cauldron ('chaudiere') — make the POT the answer. Accuracy rail: chowder originally had NO clams and NO milk (that's a later New England development) — don't project the modern dish backward. Dinner-test payoff: the 1939 Maine bill to outlaw tomatoes in chowder (T4).

topics.name: Fish & chips: Britain's national dish
topics.scope: A fried fish with a Jewish passport. T1: the 'fish' is a white fish (COD or HADDOCK) coated in BATTER and deep-fried — the batter is a jacket that steams the fish moist and soft inside while the outside crisps. T2: the fried-fish half came from SEPHARDIC JEWISH immigrants — 'pescado frito,' fish fried in batter to be eaten COLD on the Sabbath (when cooking is forbidden), brought to England from Spain and Portugal. T3: why beer or fizzy water goes in the batter — the bubbles (carbon dioxide) plus a light hand make the coating puffy and crisp rather than dense, and the batter shields the fish from the hot oil; the oil must be HOT so the crust sets fast and doesn't drink up grease. T4: the 'CHIPS' are thick-cut fried potatoes; fish and chips married up in 1860s Victorian Britain — cheap fish landed by steam trawlers plus cheap potatoes fed the industrial working class, and there were over 25,000 chip shops by 1910. T5: it mattered so much that fish and chips was one of the very few foods NEVER RATIONED in Britain during WWII — the government protected it to keep morale up (traditionally finished with MALT VINEGAR and salt).
topics.source: Wikipedia 'Fish and chips'; JTA & Times of Israel on Sephardic 'pescado frito'; Royal Museums Greenwich timeline; Joseph Malin ~1860 London shop; WWII non-rationing; 25,000+ shops by 1910.
topics.framing_note: Prep-frame welcome ('you drop battered fish into hot oil'); scene-led, never 'What is fish and chips?'. Accuracy rail: the battered-fried-fish technique is a SEPHARDIC JEWISH import (pescado frito), not a native English invention — attribute it correctly; don't overclaim the first-shop owner's ethnicity. Dinner-test payoff: the Jewish-Sabbath origin (T2) and the never-rationed-in-WWII fact (T5).

topics.name: Grits, hominy, and the corn secret
topics.scope: The Southern staple that hides a life-or-death Native technique. T1: GRITS are a Southern staple — coarsely ground CORN cooked into a hot porridge; 'hominy grits' are made from HOMINY, corn that's been treated to swell and shed its hull, not just dried field corn ground up. T2: how HOMINY is made — soak dried corn in an ALKALI (wood-ash lye, or slaked lime called 'cal'); it strips the tough hull and puffs the kernel; this ancient step is NIXTAMALIZATION (a Nahuatl word), invented by Mesoamerican peoples thousands of years ago. T3: the SAME alkali step makes MASA — the dough for corn TORTILLAS and tamales; you cannot make real tortillas from plain cornmeal, only from nixtamalized corn, because the treatment is what lets the dough hold together (grits and tortillas share one Native technique). T4: the HIDDEN nutrition — nixtamalization unlocks NIACIN (vitamin B3) that raw corn keeps locked away, plus adds calcium; Native peoples who prepared corn this way stayed healthy on a corn-heavy diet. T5: the tragic proof — Europeans adopted corn but SKIPPED the alkali step, and in the corn-dependent American South of the early 1900s that caused an epidemic of PELLAGRA (the niacin-deficiency disease of 'the four D's' — dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia, death); the step they ignored was the cure.
topics.source: Wikipedia 'Nixtamalization' & 'Hominy'; Garden & Gun 'Wood Ash Hominy'; Nahuatl etymology; niacin/pellagra link and early-20th-c. Southern pellagra epidemic.
topics.framing_note: Scene-led (corn kernels swelling in cloudy lime-water), never 'What is nixtamalization?' — teach the CONCEPT (alkali frees the nutrient), not the term as the tested answer. The controlling ACCURACY RAIL: nixtamalization is a MESOAMERICAN/Native invention (not Southern or European), and pellagra is specifically NIACIN (B3) deficiency — get both right. Keep it a food-and-nutrition beat, not a medical lecture; no microbe/enzyme Latin as the answer. Dinner-test payoff: grits and tortillas sharing one technique (T3) and the pellagra tragedy of the skipped step (T5).

topics.name: Gumbo and the roux: three cultures in one pot
topics.scope: Louisiana's melting-pot stew, deepened through its three thickeners. T1: gumbo starts with the 'HOLY TRINITY' — onion, celery, and BELL PEPPER (the Louisiana answer to French mirepoix, which uses carrot instead of pepper); this base flavors nearly every Cajun/Creole dish. T2: the very WORD 'gumbo' comes from a West African word for OKRA (Bantu 'ki ngombo'); enslaved West Africans brought okra, whose sliced pods release a natural mucilage that THICKENS the stew as it simmers. T3: the ROUX — flour cooked in fat — and the counter-intuitive rule: the DARKER you cook it (nutty, chocolate-brown for Cajun gumbo) the more it FLAVORS but the LESS it thickens, because prolonged heat breaks down the starch's thickening power. T4: FILE powder — dried, ground SASSAFRAS leaves, a gift from the CHOCTAW (Native Americans) — a third way to thicken; it's stirred in at the very END and never boiled (boiling turns it stringy/ropey). T5: CREOLE vs CAJUN — Creole ('city,' New Orleans) gumbo often has TOMATOES and leans seafood; Cajun ('country') gumbo has NO tomato and a darker roux; smoked ANDOUILLE sausage and tasso ham carry the Cajun version, and it's always served over RICE. So gumbo is literally African okra + French roux + Native filE in one bowl.
topics.source: Grokipedia 'Gumbo' (search-surfaced, direct fetch 403); Wikipedia 'Gumbo'; New Orleans School of Cooking history; etymology (Louisiana French from Bantu ngombo).
topics.framing_note: Scene-led ('a dark roux going the color of a chocolate bar'), never 'What is a roux?'. The answer is always a concrete ingredient/technique fact. Accuracy rail: the three thickeners are ALTERNATIVES (okra OR roux OR file), file is Choctaw/Native (not French), and gumbo's okra + the WORD are West African — attribute each culture correctly (active voice: name who brought what). Dinner-test payoff: the darker-roux-thickens-LESS twist (T3) and the three-cultures reveal (T5).

topics.name: Jambalaya vs paella: the saffron that wasn't there
topics.scope: Two one-pot rice dishes, one origin story. T1: paella is Spain's iconic rice dish, born in VALENCIA and cooked outdoors in a wide, shallow pan over open fire — the dish is named after the PAN ('paella'), not an ingredient; the ORIGINAL Valencian paella isn't seafood but rabbit, chicken, snails, and beans. T2: paella's golden color and flavor come from SAFFRON — the world's most expensive spice by weight, the hand-plucked crimson stigmas of a CROCUS flower (it takes thousands of flowers for an ounce). T3: SOCARRAT — the prized crisp, toasted layer of rice at the BOTTOM of the pan; you deliberately do NOT stir paella (unlike risotto) so that crust can form, and short-grain bomba rice soaks up broth while staying separate. T4: JAMBALAYA is Louisiana's rice dish — what happened when Spanish colonists tried to make paella but had NO saffron; the rice cooks IN the pot with the meat and stock (a true rice dish, unlike gumbo which is a stew ladled OVER rice). T5: 'RED' vs 'BROWN' jambalaya — Creole (New Orleans) adds TOMATOES for a red dish; Cajun uses no tomato and browns the meat for color and a brown dish — mirroring the same Creole/Cajun split as gumbo.
topics.source: Grokipedia/Wikipedia 'Paella'; Wikipedia 'Jambalaya'; Valencian paella (rice named for pan, socarrat, bomba); saffron = Crocus sativus stigmas (world's costliest spice).
topics.framing_note: INVERT THE WONDER on saffron: put 'the world's most expensive spice' in the stem and make the CROCUS FLOWER the answer (never define saffron). Scene-led throughout. Accuracy rail: paella is named after the PAN, authentic Valencian paella is rabbit/chicken/snail NOT seafood, and jambalaya descends from paella via missing saffron. Dinner-test payoff: saffron=the crocus (T2) and jambalaya-as-saffronless-paella (T4).

topics.name: Mac & cheese and the mother sauce
topics.scope: How a béchamel hides inside America's comfort food. T1: real baked mac & cheese isn't just cheese melted on noodles — it's built on a SAUCE that keeps the cheese smooth, and that sauce begins with a ROUX (flour cooked in butter). T2: whisk MILK into a roux and you get BECHAMEL, the 'white sauce' — one of the French MOTHER SAUCES; the roux thickens the milk so it clings to the pasta. T3: stir CHEESE into a bechamel and it becomes a MORNAY sauce — that is the classic mac & cheese sauce, and the roux is WHY the cheese stays creamy instead of splitting into a greasy, grainy mess (the starch stabilizes it). T4: the MOTHER SAUCE idea — French chefs (Careme, then Escoffier) sorted French sauces into a handful of 'mothers' (bechamel, veloute, espagnole, tomato, hollandaise); master one base and you can build a hundred sauces. T5: mac & cheese is far older and fancier than the blue box — a baked macaroni-and-cheese recipe appears in a 1769 English cookbook, and THOMAS JEFFERSON fell for it in Europe and served it at the White House; Kraft's boxed dinner came in 1937 as cheap Depression-era protein.
topics.source: Escoffier culinary school (five mother sauces, Le Guide Culinaire 1903); Wikipedia 'Mornay sauce' & 'Macaroni and cheese'; Elizabeth Raffald 1769 recipe; Jefferson popularization; Kraft 1937; HISTORY 'mac and cheese origins.'
topics.framing_note: Prep-frame welcome ('you whisk milk into the roux'); scene-led, never 'What is a bechamel?'. The answer is always a concrete sauce fact (roux -> bechamel -> Mornay). Accuracy rail: Mornay is bechamel PLUS cheese (classically Gruyere/Parmesan; cheddar in the American version) — get the build order right; Jefferson popularized but did NOT invent it. Dinner-test payoff: the roux is what keeps cheese from going oily/grainy (T3), plus Jefferson's White House mac & cheese (T5).

topics.name: New England lobster and the clambake
topics.scope: The trash food that became a luxury, cooked the Native way. T1: LOBSTER was once POVERTY FOOD in colonial New England — so absurdly abundant it piled up on the shore after storms; it was fed to prisoners, servants, and the poor and used as fertilizer and fish bait, not prized at all. T2: the flip — canning and then the RAILROAD (shipping live lobster inland and serving it in dining cars to travelers who didn't know it was 'cheap') turned lobster into a luxury by the late 1800s; scarcity plus marketing reversed its status. T3: the CLAMBAKE technique came from Northeastern Native Americans (the Wampanoag) — dig a pit, heat STONES red-hot in a fire, pile on wet SEAWEED; the trapped seawater STEAMS the clams, lobster, and corn with no pot at all; settlers copied it. T4: why a lobster's shell turns RED when cooked — the shell hides a red pigment (astaxanthin) clamped inside a protein that masks it as drab blue-brown camouflage; heat unfolds the protein and lets the red show.
topics.source: HISTORY '7 Things About Lobsters'; historyfacts.com (colonial lobster as prisoner food); Wikipedia 'Clambake' & Britannica (Wampanoag hot-stone-and-seaweed steaming); astaxanthin/crustacyanin color-change chemistry.
topics.framing_note: Scene-led (lobster washing up in two-foot piles; stones glowing in a beach pit); never 'What is a clambake?'. Accuracy rail: the clambake is a NATIVE (Wampanoag/Algonquian) technique the settlers adopted — attribute it correctly. Keep the shell-color rung a clean single mechanism (pigment freed by heat), no Latin enzyme names as the answer. Dinner-test payoff: lobster-was-trash-food (T1) and the shell-turns-red reveal (T4).

topics.name: Soul food: brilliance from the scraps
topics.scope: The honest, food-anchored origin of soul food. T1: soul food grew from the cooking of enslaved African Americans, who were handed the plantation's cast-off cuts and turned them into something delicious — chitterlings (pig intestines, cleaned and slow-cooked), pig's feet, ham hocks. T2: the WEST AFRICAN pantry that crossed the Atlantic — okra, black-eyed peas, yams, sorghum, rice, watermelon — carried on slave ships and rooted into Southern cooking. T3: COLLARD GREENS and 'POTLIKKER' — tough greens slow-simmered with a smoked ham hock, and the vitamin-rich cooking liquid left behind ('pot liquor') was saved, not tossed, and sopped up with cornbread (an honest nutrition truth: nutrients leach into the broth). T4: the GREAT MIGRATION — roughly six million Black Americans left the rural South for Chicago, Detroit, Harlem, Philadelphia (1910-1970), carrying these dishes north, where soul-food restaurants opened. T5: the NAME — 'soul food' was coined in the 1960s, when 'soul' stood for Black pride and culture (soul music, soul food); the name was a declaration of dignity for a cuisine born of hardship; black-eyed peas and greens eaten on New Year's for luck and money.
topics.source: Wikipedia 'Soul food' & 'List of soul foods'; USC Scribe and Tennessee Lookout histories; Great Migration figures (~6M, 1910-1970); term coined mid-1960s.
topics.framing_note: Handle with dignity and ACTIVE VOICE — name that enslavers gave over the unwanted cuts (don't passive-voice the slavery), and celebrate the resourcefulness without romanticizing the suffering. Food-anchored answers only (a cut, an ingredient, potlikker, the coined name) — never a bare date or policy. Scene-led. Accuracy rail: the West African ingredients (okra, black-eyed peas, yams) are genuinely African imports; cornbread's corn is Native American — attribute origins correctly. Dinner-test payoff: potlikker being saved for its nutrients (T3) and the 1960s name-as-declaration (T5). vision_mandated TRUE: this ladder turns on the bank's honest-history + active-voice-responsibility stance.

topics.name: The Cornish pasty
topics.scope: A miner's lunch with a built-in handle. T1: the Cornish pasty is a hand-held meat pie from Cornwall — beef, potato, SWEDE (rutabaga), and onion sealed RAW in pastry and baked so the filling cooks in its own steam; it was the TIN MINER'S portable lunch. T2: the thick CRIMPED ridge along the side is a HANDLE — the traditional story is that miners with dirty (sometimes arsenic-dusted) hands gripped the crimp, ate the rest, and threw the handle away, keeping the food clean. T3: the name is now LEGALLY protected — since 2011 a 'Cornish pasty' has PGI status: to use the name it must be the 'D' shape, crimped on the SIDE (never over the top), made in Cornwall with the traditional filling — a top-crimped one isn't the real thing.
topics.source: Wikipedia 'Pasty'; Historic UK 'History of the Cornish Pasty'; EU PGI status (2011): D-shape, side-crimp, Cornwall, beef/potato/swede/onion.
topics.framing_note: Scene-led (a miner underground holding the crimp), never 'What is a Cornish pasty?'. Accuracy rail: present the throw-away-the-handle detail as the TRADITIONAL STORY (some historians dispute it — food was too precious to waste), but the PGI facts (D-shape, side-crimp, Cornwall) are settled law — keep those firm. Dinner-test payoff: the crimp-as-handle (T2) and the side-crimp legal rule (T3).

topics.name: The Sunday roast and Yorkshire pudding
topics.scope: Wasting nothing under a roasting joint. T1: the British Sunday roast centers on a roasted joint of BEEF; as it cooks, fat and juices drip down, and cooks set a pan beneath it to catch the 'DRIPPING' so nothing is wasted. T2: YORKSHIRE PUDDING is not a dessert — it's a savory batter (flour, egg, milk) poured into that hot beef DRIPPING and roasted until it puffs into a crisp, hollow shell; it was originally called 'dripping pudding.' T3: the RISE mechanism — the fat must be SMOKING hot when the batter hits it; the water in the batter flashes to STEAM and blows the pudding up into a hollow dome (a cold pan gives a flat, greasy pudding). T4: WHY it exists — a thrifty way to stretch an expensive roast; the pudding was traditionally served FIRST, before the meat, so people filled up on cheap batter and a little beef went further; the name was fixed by Hannah Glasse's 1747 cookbook.
topics.source: Wikipedia 'Yorkshire pudding'; Grokipedia 'Yorkshire pudding' (search-surfaced); 'A Dripping Pudding' in The Whole Duty of a Woman (1737); Hannah Glasse, The Art of Cookery (1747).
topics.framing_note: Prep-frame welcome ('you pour cold batter into smoking-hot dripping'); scene-led, never 'What is Yorkshire pudding?'. Accuracy rail: the rise is STEAM-driven (flashing water), not a chemical leavener like baking powder — the answer must teach steam. Dinner-test payoff: the served-FIRST-to-stretch-the-beef trick (T4) and the steam-rise reveal (T3).

topics.name: The four BBQ regions
topics.scope: America's BBQ map — the styles that disagree on meat AND sauce. T1: American BBQ splits by REGION, and the first split is the MEAT — Texas is BEEF country (brisket) thanks to its cattle ranching, while most of the South smokes PORK. T2: the CAROLINAS smoke pork (Eastern NC does the WHOLE HOG) and dress it with a thin VINEGAR-and-pepper sauce — no thick tomato sauce at all; the vinegar cuts the fat. T3: KANSAS CITY is the sweet, thick, TOMATO-and-MOLASSES sauce most people picture when they hear 'BBQ sauce,' and its signature dish is BURNT ENDS — the twice-smoked fatty point end of the brisket, once thrown away. T4: MEMPHIS is a pork-RIB town famous for the 'DRY' rub — ribs crusted in spice and served with NO sauce (vs 'wet' mopped ribs). T5: the odd one out — South Carolina's mustard-gold 'Carolina Gold' sauce, a legacy of German immigrant settlers; and central-Texas brisket's plain salt-and-pepper 'Dalmatian' rub from old German/Czech butcher-shop 'meat markets.'
topics.source: Grokipedia 'Barbecue' (search-surfaced); Wikipedia 'Barbecue in the United States,' 'Burnt ends,' 'Carolina-style barbecue'; regional BBQ references corroborating meat/sauce splits.
topics.framing_note: Answer is always a concrete meat-or-sauce fact tied to a named PLACE (beef=Texas, vinegar=Carolinas, sweet tomato+burnt ends=KC, dry rub=Memphis). Scene-led, never 'What sauce does X use?' as a definition shell — set the scene (a whole hog on the coals, a rib with no sauce) and make the region/technique the known answer. Accuracy rail: burnt ends come from the brisket POINT and were originally scraps, not a premium cut invented on purpose. Dinner-test payoff: burnt ends being reclaimed trimmings, and the mustard-gold German-Carolina outlier.

topics.name: The pie: from meat 'coffin' to apple pie
topics.scope: How a container became a dessert. T1: the first pies were SAVORY, and the crust wasn't meant to be eaten — a thick flour-and-water shell called a 'COFFIN' (coffyn) that sealed meat inside; it was edible-ish packaging, not a treat. T2: WHY the coffin worked — baked rock-hard, it sealed the meat from air and trapped the juices, letting a pie KEEP and TRAVEL for weeks before refrigeration (medieval Tupperware); people ate the filling and often discarded or fed out the tough crust. T3: the crusts diverged by JOB — a stiff HOT-WATER crust (fat + boiling water) stands on its own for a standing pie like a pork pie, while a flaky SHORTCRUST works by cutting COLD fat into flour so it stays in flakes; keeping the fat cold is the whole secret to 'flaky.' T4: BLIND BAKING — you pre-bake an empty bottom crust (weighted down with dried beans or pie weights) so a wet filling can't leave it raw and 'soggy-bottomed.' T5: 'as American as apple pie' — except apples AREN'T native to America (Europeans brought them; only sour crabapples grew wild) and apple pie is medieval ENGLISH; PUMPKIN, a true native American squash, makes the more genuinely 'American' pie.
topics.source: Atlas Obscura 'Medieval Europeans... Pastry Coffins'; Matador Network 'Coffin-Inspired History of Pie Crust'; Wikipedia 'Pie' & 'Hot water crust pastry'; apple domestication (Old World / Malus origins).
topics.framing_note: Prep-frame welcome ('you cut cold butter into the flour'); scene-led, never 'What is a pie?'. The controlling ACCURACY RAIL: apples are an OLD WORLD import to the Americas (only crabapples were native), so 'as American as apple pie' is a fond myth — the answer must land that, with pumpkin as the truly native pie. Also: the 'coffin' crust was often NOT eaten. Dinner-test payoff: the apple-pie-isn't-American reveal (T5) and the coffin-as-Tupperware origin (T1-T2).

topics.name: The sandwich and the Earl
topics.scope: The food named after a man, and the myth about him. T1: the sandwich is named after a PERSON — John Montagu, the 4th Earl of SANDWICH (Sandwich being a town in England); the food took his aristocratic title. T2: the famous legend — around 1762 the Earl, a compulsive card player, refused to leave the gambling table to eat, so he had meat brought between two slices of bread he could hold in one hand without greasing the cards; other gamblers began ordering 'the same as Sandwich.' T3: label the LEGEND as legend — the gambling story comes from a gossipy French travel writer years after the fact; historians think the Earl, a hard-working First Lord of the Admiralty, more likely ate it at his WORK DESK; the earliest written mention is in Edward Gibbon's 1762 diary. T4: the IDEA is far older than the name — Hillel the Elder wrapped Passover lamb and bitter herbs in flatbread around the 1st century BC; the Earl gave the English-speaking world the NAME, not the invention.
topics.source: HISTORY 'Who Invented the Sandwich?'; Wikipedia 'John Montagu, 4th Earl of Sandwich'; Edward Gibbon 1762 diary (earliest written use); Pierre-Jean Grosley's Tour to London (gambling-table story, early 1770s).
topics.framing_note: Scene-led (the smoky card room, greasy fingers on the cards). The controlling ACCURACY RAIL: the gambling-table tale is a LATER legend — the stem may tell it as 'the story goes,' but the ladder must also carry the desk-at-the-Admiralty alternative and the Gibbon-diary fact, and no rung may assert the gambling story as settled truth. Dinner-test payoff: the T3 debunk (probably his work desk, not the card table) and T4's older-than-its-name (Hillel).

topics.name: Cantonese cooking — dim sum and the steamer
topics.scope: Cantonese cuisine chases FRESHNESS and turned tea-time snacks into an art. T1: dim sum is a meal of many small SHARED plates eaten with tea; the whole custom is called yum cha, literally 'drink tea.' T2: the plates arrive stacked in bamboo STEAMERS — steaming, a gentle wet heat, is a Cantonese signature because it cooks delicately without masking a food's own flavor. T3: the star dumpling, har gow, has a translucent skin made from WHEAT STARCH (not ordinary flour) — that's what turns see-through and pleasantly chewy when steamed. T4: Cantonese cooking prizes an ingredient's own freshness above heavy sauces — a whole fish is steamed just until done, then finished simply with ginger, scallion, and a splash of hot oil, never drowned. T5: the tradition grew from teahouses along old trade roads in Guangdong, where travelers stopped to rest, sip tea, and nibble — the snacks slowly became a cuisine of their own.
topics.source: Grokipedia checked first — corroborated via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dim_sum, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yum_cha, discoverhongkong.com 'Heavenly Kings of Dim Sum', dimsumpalace.com Cantonese guide.
topics.framing_note: Scene-led from the rolling cart and stacked bamboo steamers. Accuracy rails: dim sum / yum cha is Cantonese (Guangdong and Hong Kong); har gow's clear wrapper is wheat STARCH, not rice paper. Payoff rung is T3 (the see-through dumpling skin is wheat starch).

topics.name: Chili's journey into Asia (the Columbian Exchange)
topics.scope: The fiery red of Asian food is a plot twist only ~400 years old. T1: a chili's burn isn't heat at all — it's capsaicin, a chemical that tricks the same nerves that sense scalding, so your brain thinks your mouth is hot. T2: chili peppers are a NEW WORLD plant — domesticated in the Americas (Mexico and the Andes) and completely unknown in Asia before Columbus. T2: Portuguese traders carried chili around Africa to India and East Asia in the 1500s (part of the Columbian Exchange). T3: before chili arrived, 'spicy' Sichuan food leaned on the numbing Sichuan pepper plus ginger and mustard — the fiery-red identity we picture is barely 300 years old (Hunan first records chili in 1684). T3: Korea folded chili into kimchi and gochujang only after ~1600 — older kimchi was white and non-spicy. T4: most of a chili's heat lives in the white inner rib/pith, NOT the seeds as people assume; that heat is measured on the Scoville scale. T4: birds feel no burn from capsaicin and spread the seeds far and wide — the plant 'aims' its heat at seed-crushing mammals, so the burn is really a defense. T5: because capsaicin binds the body's real heat-sensor (TRPV1), your brain literally can't tell chili from a burn — the endorphin rush afterward is why people crave it. T5: chili tolerance is learned, not inborn — enjoying pain-that-can't-hurt-you is sometimes called 'benign masochism.'
topics.source: Grokipedia checked first — corroborated via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chili_pepper, thebeijinger.com 'How the Beloved Chili Arrived in China', scmp.com 'How Asians embraced the chilli pepper', splendidtable.org 'How chili peppers conquered the world'; capsaicin/TRPV1 pharmacology (general consensus).
topics.framing_note: Food-driven history where the CHILI itself is always the anchor (no bare trade policy). Flagship accuracy rail: chili is a New World plant unknown in Asia before ~1500 — 'Asian food was always fiery-red' is FALSE (Portuguese carried it east in the 1500s; Hunan 1684, Sichuan ~1749). Attribute domestication to the Americas. Dates/Scoville numbers are context, never the tested answer. Payoff rung is T4 (birds feel no burn and spread the seeds — the heat is aimed at mammals).

topics.name: Dashi and the discovery of umami
topics.scope: The savory base under nearly all Japanese cooking — and the taste it revealed. T1: dashi is the clear broth beneath miso soup and countless Japanese dishes — made simply from kombu (kelp) and shavings of dried fish (bonito, katsuobushi). T1: it delivers a deep savory, mouth-filling taste that isn't salty, sweet, sour, or bitter. T2: that taste is umami, now recognized as the fifth basic taste; the kelp supplies it through glutamate (an amino acid). T3: in 1908 the chemist Kikunae Ikeda isolated glutamate from kombu and named the taste umami ('pleasant savory taste'). T3: bonito flakes bring a SECOND savory molecule, inosinate, from the fish. T4: glutamate and inosinate together taste far MORE savory than either alone — 'umami synergy' multiplies rather than adds, which is exactly why the kombu-plus-bonito pairing became the classic. T4: the same glutamate is naturally rich in parmesan, ripe tomatoes, mushrooms, and cured ham — which is why those foods taste 'savory' the world over. T5: MSG is simply that same glutamate isolated as a salt — the identical molecule found in kombu and tomato; the mid-century scare that blamed it for illness was never substantiated. T5: katsuobushi is among the hardest foods on earth — bonito that's smoked, dried, and mold-fermented into a wood-like block, then shaved paper-thin.
topics.source: Grokipedia checked first — corroborated via umamiinfo.com 'What is Dashi'/'What is Umami', en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kikunae_Ikeda, ajinomoto.com 'Who Identified Umami and When', ice.edu 'How Dashi Led to the Discovery of MSG', ramenchemistry.com 'Umami Synergy'.
topics.framing_note: Scene-led from a bowl of miso soup and that 'savory-but-not-salty' puzzle. Accuracy rails: Ikeda IDENTIFIED and NAMED umami in 1908 (do not say he 'invented' the taste); MSG is the SAME glutamate found in kombu, tomato, and parmesan and the old scare was never substantiated (settled nutrition, not a contested stance). BANNED: the tested answer is never the exact 1:1 ratio or a Latin name — teach the concept (kelp gives glutamate, fish gives inosinate, together they multiply). Payoff rung is T4 (the two-molecule synergy / the same glutamate hides in parmesan and tomato).

topics.name: Kimchi — Korea's living, fermenting dish
topics.scope: The science behind the fizzy, sour, spicy cabbage. T1: kimchi is cabbage preserved by FERMENTATION, not by cooking or canning — it keeps for months and grows more sour the longer it sits. T2: step one is salting/brining the napa cabbage — the salt pulls water out and creates conditions where only the GOOD microbes can thrive. T3: those microbes (lactobacillus, the same family that sours yogurt and sauerkraut) eat the cabbage's sugars and make lactic acid — that's the tangy sourness and the gentle fizz. T4: the fiery RED kimchi we picture is only ~400 years old — before chili reached Korea, kimchi was white and non-spicy (baek-kimchi still is). T5: families once buried sealed pots underground for a steady cool temperature all winter (the kimjang tradition); modern Korean homes keep a dedicated kimchi refrigerator instead.
topics.source: Grokipedia checked first — corroborated via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kimchi, revolutionfermentation.com '9 Amazing Facts About Kimchi', tastekoreanfood.com 'Kimchi Fermentation & Kimjang'.
topics.framing_note: Matter-of-fact prep voice. Accuracy rails: spicy red kimchi is post-~1600 (chili is a New World plant) and older kimchi was non-spicy; lacto-fermentation is the SAME process as yogurt and sauerkraut. BANNED: no Latin species name as the tested answer — teach the concept (salt selects good microbes; they make lactic acid). Payoff rung is T4 (kimchi wasn't always red or spicy).

topics.name: Koji — the mold behind soy sauce and miso
topics.scope: How a friendly mold turns bland soybeans into the savory backbone of East Asian cooking. T1: soy sauce and miso aren't simply cooked — they're FERMENTED, aged for months from soybeans. T2: the secret worker is koji, a cultivated mold grown on steamed grain or beans — so central to the cuisine it's honored as Japan's 'national fungus.' T3: the mold's enzymes slowly chop the soybean's big, flavorless proteins into small savory pieces — including glutamate, the umami molecule — so time and mold accomplish what no knife or fire can. T4: soy sauce is soybeans plus roasted WHEAT plus salty brine, fermented as a mash and aged; miso is a thick soybean paste fermented with koji-grain — same mold, different texture and time. T5: this is why a spoon of miso or a splash of soy sauce makes almost anything taste 'meatier' — you're adding concentrated glutamate, the very same savory molecule as in dashi. T5: tamari is the wheat-free soy sauce — a byproduct of miso-making, thicker and rounder than regular soy sauce.
topics.source: Grokipedia checked first — corroborated via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aspergillus_oryzae, mdpi.com 'Japanese Traditional Miso and Koji Making', umamiinfo.com 'Miso', pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov soy-sauce koji studies.
topics.framing_note: Kitchen/prep voice is fine ('you stir in a spoon of miso'). BANNED: the tested answer is never the mold's Latin name (Aspergillus oryzae) or a salt/brine percentage — teach the CONCEPT that fermentation unlocks glutamate. Accuracy rail: soy sauce contains WHEAT (not soy alone); these are fermented, not steeped like tea. Payoff rung is T3 (the mold's enzymes create the umami glutamate — the same molecule as dashi).

topics.name: Korean BBQ — banchan, ssam and the grill table
topics.scope: A Korean BBQ table is a build-it-yourself meal. T1: the cooking happens AT the table — diners grill strips of meat on a grill set into the tabletop itself. T2: the meat is never the whole meal — it comes surrounded by banchan, a spread of small SIDE dishes (kimchi, pickled radish, seasoned greens) that are refilled for free. T3: you eat it as ssam, a 'wrap': lay grilled meat on a lettuce or perilla leaf, add rice, raw garlic, and a dab of ssamjang (a savory-spicy fermented paste), then fold it and eat in one bite. T4: bulgogi ('fire meat') is marinated before grilling — and Korean cooks often grate ASIAN PEAR into the marinade because the fruit's enzymes tenderize the beef while adding a clean sweetness. T5: the deep savory-spicy base of many Korean sauces is gochujang, a fermented chili-and-soybean paste — and its chili, like kimchi's, only arrived in Korea about 400 years ago.
topics.source: Grokipedia checked first — corroborated via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ssam, tastekoreanfood.com 'Banchan for Korean BBQ', afar.com 'What Korean BBQ Is and How to Eat It'; pear-enzyme tenderizing (general food science).
topics.framing_note: Prep / at-the-table voice. Accuracy rails: gochujang's chili is post-~1600 (New World plant); the Asian-pear enzyme tenderizing is a real mechanism, not folklore. Payoff rung is T4 (grated Asian pear tenderizes bulgogi).

topics.name: Malà — Sichuan's numbing pepper
topics.scope: The 'other' spicy — why Sichuan food buzzes as well as burns. T1: Sichuan cooking has TWO sensations, not one — a chili burn (là) AND a strange tingling numbness (má); together they're called málà. T2: the numbness comes from the Sichuan peppercorn, which despite its name is not a chili and not related to black pepper — it's the dried husk of a fruit in the CITRUS family (Zanthoxylum). T3: it doesn't hit heat/pain nerves like chili does — it fools your TOUCH nerves, so your lips feel like they're lightly vibrating or fluttering (the compound is sanshool; the buzz clocks near 50 taps a second). T4: cooks pair the numbing pepper WITH chili on purpose — the numbness dulls the mouth just enough that you can enjoy more chili heat without being overwhelmed. T5: this doubled sensation is the backbone of the classic dishes — mapo tofu and Chongqing hotpot are built on málà oil.
topics.source: Grokipedia checked first — corroborated via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sichuan_pepper, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydroxy-%CE%B1-sanshool, smithsonianmag.com 'Why Szechuan Peppers Make Your Lips Go Numb', 50hertzfoods.com on málà.
topics.framing_note: Invert the wonder: lead with the buzzing-lips sensation, make the citrus-family husk the answer. Accuracy rails: Sichuan pepper is NOT a chili or a true peppercorn (it's a Zanthoxylum husk), and it acts on TOUCH nerves not heat receptors; the '~50 taps a second' stays CONTEXT, never the tested answer (no bare number as answer). The chili half is New World — see the chili-into-Asia ladder. Payoff rung is T2 (it's a citrus relative, not pepper at all).

topics.name: Peking duck — engineering shatter-crisp skin
topics.scope: The whole dish is built around one thing: glassy, crackling skin. T1: at the table the prize of Peking duck isn't the meat — it's the paper-thin, shatteringly crisp SKIN. T2: to get there, cooks first separate skin from meat by pumping AIR under the skin so it balloons away from the flesh. T3: the duck is then hung to AIR-DRY for many hours — dry skin crisps in the oven, while damp skin only steams and turns leathery. T4: before roasting, the skin is brushed with a MALTOSE (malt-sugar) syrup — in the heat that sugar browns into the signature mahogany, lacquered sheen (Maillard and caramelization at work). T5: it's an imperial dish perfected in Ming-dynasty Beijing kitchens; the crisp skin is served wrapped in thin pancakes with scallion, cucumber, and sweet hoisin-style sauce.
topics.source: Grokipedia checked first — corroborated via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peking_duck, nationalgeographic.com 'Peking duck: the complex history', pagefacts.com 'Peking Duck Facts'.
topics.framing_note: Prep/technique voice is the point (the game action is cooking). Accuracy rails: Ming-dynasty imperial origin; the glaze is maltose (malt sugar) and the color is Maillard/caramel, not literal paint. Payoff rung is T2 (air is pumped under the skin to separate it from the meat).

topics.name: Ramen — a Chinese import turned Japanese icon
topics.scope: Japan's most famous bowl started somewhere else. T1: ramen is a wheat-NOODLE soup — the noodles matter every bit as much as the broth. T2: those springy, faintly YELLOW noodles get their bounce and color from kansui, an alkaline (soda) water worked into the dough — plain-water wheat noodles simply won't behave that way. T3: ramen came FROM China — in the early 1900s Japan called it 'Chinese soba' (chuka soba); it is not an ancient Japanese dish. T4: the broth STYLE names the bowl — tonkotsu, for instance, is pork bones boiled so hard and long that fat and collagen emulsify into a creamy, cloudy-white soup. T5: in 1958 Momofuku Ando invented INSTANT ramen — flash-fried dried noodles rehydrated with boiling water — later voted Japan's greatest invention of the 20th century.
topics.source: Grokipedia checked first — corroborated via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramen, britannica.com/topic/ramen, history.com 'Momofuku Ando creates first mass-market instant ramen (1958)'.
topics.framing_note: Scene-led from the bowl. Accuracy rails: ramen is Chinese-derived (arrived early 20th c.), NOT ancient Japanese; instant ramen is 1958 (Momofuku Ando). BANNED: no chemical name as the tested answer — teach the concept (alkaline water makes the springy yellow noodle). Payoff rung is T3 (ramen is originally Chinese) with T5 (instant ramen) as the fun close.

topics.name: Stir-fry logic and velveting
topics.scope: Why a good stir-fry needs a plan before the heat comes on. T1: a stir-fry cooks in just two or three minutes, so there's no time to chop mid-cook — everything is cut and measured FIRST, then cooked in a rush. T2: ingredients go into the wok by how long they need — aromatics like garlic and ginger first, then meat, then hardy vegetables, sauce last — so nothing ends up raw or overcooked. T3: crowding the wok is the enemy — too much food at once cools the pan and everything STEAMS grey instead of searing, so cooks work in small batches to keep it screaming hot and dry. T4: restaurant meat is silky because of VELVETING — the raw meat is coated in cornstarch, often with egg white, forming a slick shell that seals in juices and stays tender. T5: a pinch of BAKING SODA in the marinade raises the meat's pH, which keeps its proteins from clenching tight in the heat — that's the real trick behind impossibly tender stir-fried beef.
topics.source: Grokipedia checked first — corroborated via woksoflove.com stir-fry technique guides and general Chinese-cooking food science (velveting = cornstarch/egg-white coat; baking soda raises pH to tenderize).
topics.framing_note: Prep-voice is ideal (the game action IS cooking). Accuracy rails: velveting is a cornstarch/egg-white coat; baking soda tenderizes via pH — a real mechanism, not a myth. BANNED: no exact percentages or gram amounts as the tested answer — teach the concept. Payoff rung is T5 (baking soda's pH trick for melt-tender beef).

topics.name: Sushi: from preservation to nigiri
topics.scope: The surprising truth about what 'sushi' actually is. T1: sushi does NOT mean raw fish — the raw fish on its own is sashimi; 'sushi' names the seasoned, vinegared RICE (the '-su-' points to vinegar and sourness). T1: nigiri is a hand-pressed finger of that vinegared rice with a topping laid over it. T2: sushi began as a way to PRESERVE fish, not as a fresh delicacy. T2: the ancient method (narezushi) packed cleaned fish in salt and cooked rice and let it ferment for months; the sour, lactic fermentation is what kept the fish edible without refrigeration. T3: in the oldest form the fermented RICE was thrown away — only the preserved fish was eaten (funazushi near Lake Biwa is still made this way). T3: over centuries people began eating the tangy rice too, not just the fish. T4: Edo-period cooks swapped the slow fermentation for a quick splash of rice VINEGAR — instant sourness, no months of waiting. T4: in 1820s Edo (old Tokyo) the cook Hanaya Yohei served hand-pressed nigiri as fast STREET FOOD — the direct ancestor of today's sushi bar. T5: wasabi and pickled ginger aren't only for flavor — both have antimicrobial properties that pair naturally with once-raw fish. T5: the vinegared rice, not the refrigerator, was the ORIGINAL safety technology — acid slows spoilage.
topics.source: Grokipedia checked first — corroborated via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_sushi, bokksu.com 'Narezushi: The Origins', briandcolwell.com 'A Complete History of Sushi'; funazushi/Kitashina and Hanaya Yohei (1799-1858, nigiri c.1824) per History of sushi.
topics.framing_note: Invert the cliche: hook on 'sushi = raw fish?' and make the vinegared RICE the answer. Accuracy rails: sushi refers to the seasoned rice (raw fish alone is sashimi); nigiri is an 1820s Edo invention, NOT ancient (no anachronism); the oldest narezushi discarded the fermented rice. Payoff rung is T3 (the original sushi threw the rice away and ate only the preserved fish).

topics.name: Tempura — the Portuguese gift to Japan
topics.scope: Japan's lacy fried shrimp is a foreign transplant. T1: tempura is seafood and vegetables dipped in a thin batter and deep-fried until pale, lacy, and crisp — light, never heavy or bready. T2: it isn't originally Japanese — Portuguese missionaries brought the batter-frying technique to Nagasaki in the 1500s, and the name likely traces to the Latin 'tempora,' the Catholic fasting days when they ate battered vegetables instead of meat. T3: the trademark lacy, non-greasy crust comes from the batter being ICE-COLD and barely mixed — minimal stirring means little gluten forms, so it fries into a delicate shell rather than a thick, doughy coat.
topics.source: Grokipedia checked first — corroborated via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tempura, michelin (guide.michelin.com) 'The History of Tempura', aleteia.org 'The surprising Catholic origins of tempura'.
topics.framing_note: A food-history gem. Accuracy rail: tempura is Portuguese-INTRODUCED (16th-c. Nanban trade), NOT indigenous or ancient Japanese; the name traces to Latin 'tempora' (fasting days). Payoff rung is T2 (tempura came from Portugal). The batter-science rung teaches the gluten concept in plain words, no jargon.

topics.name: Tofu — cheese-logic for the soybean
topics.scope: Tofu is dairy-cheese thinking applied to a bean. T1: tofu is made from soy 'milk' — soybeans soaked, ground, boiled, and strained into a creamy white liquid. T2: to turn that milk into a solid block you add a COAGULANT that makes the proteins clump and set — exactly the way cheese is curdled from dairy milk. T3: the classic coagulants are nigari (a bitter mineral salt left from seawater) or gypsum (a chalky calcium mineral) — a small pinch sets a whole pot. T4: how hard you press out the watery whey decides the result — barely set is silky, custard-soft tofu; pressed firm is the block you can cube, fry, or grill. T5: by legend a Han-dynasty prince, Liu An, discovered tofu some 2,000 years ago in China; the delicate skin that forms atop simmering soy milk is skimmed off as yuba (tofu skin), a delicacy of its own.
topics.source: Grokipedia grokipedia.com/page/Tofu checked first (page exists; WebFetch 403-blocked) — corroborated via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tofu, ift.org 'How Tofu Is Processed', soyinfocenter.com 'History of Tofu'.
topics.framing_note: Prep voice is fine. Accuracy rails: label the Liu An origin as LEGEND, not settled history; tofu is Chinese (Han-era). BANNED: chemical formulas or set-percentages as the tested answer — teach the concept (a coagulant clumps the protein, just like curdling cheese). Payoff rung is T2 (tofu is curdled like cheese — same idea, made from plant milk).

topics.name: Wok hei — the breath of the wok
topics.scope: Why a restaurant stir-fry tastes smoky-charred in a way a home pan can't match. T1: a wok is round-bottomed so food slides to a screaming-hot center and up the cooler sides — you toss constantly so nothing sits and steams. T2: a carbon-steel wok builds a black non-stick 'seasoning' patina from oil polymerizing onto the metal over time. T2: crowding the wok is the enemy — pile in too much and the pan cools, so food STEAMS grey instead of searing (dry heat browns, wet heat doesn't). T3: 'wok hei' (breath of the wok) is a distinct smoky aroma — not from charcoal but from the food and oil searing at ferocious heat. T3: the browning is the Maillard reaction — amino acids plus sugars rearranging into hundreds of roasty flavor compounds (same reaction that browns toast and seared steak). T4: the signature smokiness comes from the OIL: near 300C+ droplets aerosolize into a mist that briefly ignites over the flame and settles back onto the food as toasted-oil flavor. T5: home stoves rarely get hot enough — a restaurant wok burner roars at many times a home stove's output, which is why 'wok hei' is so hard to fake at home. T5: it stops just short of burning — the char flavor arrives while the food itself stays tender, a razor's-edge of heat and timing.
topics.source: Grokipedia grokipedia.com/page/Wok_hei checked first (page exists; WebFetch 403-blocked) — corroborated via headcountcoffee.com 'The Science Behind Stir-Frying', misterwok.net/journal/wok-hei-physics, woksoflove.com 'How to Get Wok Hei at Home', ricebowldeluxe.com; Maillard reaction (general food-science consensus).
topics.framing_note: Scene-led from the smoky restaurant plate; make the KNOWABLE cause the answer. Accuracy rail: wok hei is oil-aerosol combustion + Maillard, NOT charcoal smoke and NOT 'burnt' — it stops just short of char. Prep-voice ('you toss it over the flame') is fine. Payoff rung is T4 (the oil catches fire mid-air and rains flavor back onto the food).

topics.name: Beef Wellington
topics.scope: The showpiece roast wrapped in pastry - and the engineering that keeps the pastry crisp. T1: Beef Wellington wraps a whole beef fillet (tenderloin) in pastry and bakes it - the grandest 'meat in a blanket'. T2a: between the meat and the pastry is a layer of finely chopped mushrooms cooked down dry (duxelles). T2b: the classic wreck is a SOGGY BOTTOM - juices from the meat soaking into the pastry. T3a: the fix is that the duxelles (plus a wrap of prosciutto or a thin crepe) acts as a moisture BARRIER, soaking up meat juices so the pastry stays crisp. T3b: 'en croute' means 'in a crust' - Beef Wellington is essentially the French filet de boeuf en croute under a British name. T4: nobody can actually prove it's named for the Duke of Wellington - food historians think it's a patriotic rebrand of the French en-croute dish.
topics.source: Grokipedia checked first (403); corroborated via Wikipedia 'Beef Wellington' (beef tenderloin + mushroom duxelles + puff pastry; prosciutto wrap retains moisture and prevents soggy pastry; 'presumably' named for Arthur Wellesley but connection unknown; historian Leah Hyslop - patriotic rebrand of filet de boeuf en croute).
topics.framing_note: Dish ladder built around ONE mechanism payoff (the moisture barrier). Scene-led - set the 'soggy bottom' PROBLEM in the stem without revealing the barrier fix (anti-restatement: the player must know the duxelles/prosciutto solves it). ACCURACY RAIL: the Duke-of-Wellington naming is uncertain/unproven - frame T4's answer as the FOOD fact (it's the same dish as French filet de boeuf en croute), not the Duke's name. Dinner-test payoff = T3a (the duxelles moisture barrier). Prep-frame voice fine.

topics.name: Caramelized onions and French onion soup
topics.scope: The browning that turns sharp onions sweet - and why it's NOT the same as a seared steak. T1: French onion soup's deep brown color and sweet flavor come from cooking onions LOW and SLOW for a long time, not from any broth coloring. T2a: as onions cook, their natural SUGARS brown - that's caramelization, and it's why long-cooked onions taste sweet instead of sharp. T2b: the soup is finished 'gratinee' - a raft of bread and melted Gruyere browned under the broiler. T3a: caramelization is just SUGAR browning with heat - the same reaction that makes creme brulee's crust and tarte Tatin's color. T3b: caramelization is NOT the Maillard reaction - Maillard needs protein (it's what browns a seared steak or bread crust); caramelization is sugar alone. T4: tarte Tatin is the upside-down apple tart where apples caramelize in butter and sugar in the pan, then the whole thing is flipped - and the 'happy accident' origin story is mostly legend.
topics.source: Grokipedia checked first (403); corroborated via Wikipedia 'French onion soup' (slowly sauteed/caramelized onions in meat stock, gratineed with bread + cheese; Les Halles Paris, mid-19thc) and 'Tarte Tatin' (apples caramelized in butter+sugar then inverted; Tatin sisters at Lamotte-Beuvron; the accident narrative is largely mythical). Build-stage ref: McGee (caramelization = sugar pyrolysis vs Maillard = amino acid + reducing sugar).
topics.framing_note: Mechanism ladder anchored on a dish - reveal caramelization and, as the sharp payoff, its difference from Maillard. Scene-led ('what makes onion soup sweet and brown?'). ACCURACY RAILS: two, both baked in as payoffs - caramelization (sugar) is distinct from Maillard (needs protein), and the tarte Tatin accident story is LEGEND. Prep-frame voice fine. Dinner-test payoff = T3b (caramelization vs Maillard - a bright 15-year-old can reason it). Keep all four choices live; don't name the reaction in the stem.

topics.name: Choux pastry (eclairs and cream puffs)
topics.scope: The one dough behind a whole family of hollow French pastries. T1: an eclair or cream puff is HOLLOW inside - that empty dome is the whole point, built to be filled with cream. T2a: choux is the strange dough you cook TWICE - first as a paste on the stovetop, then baked. T2b: it puffs with no yeast and no baking powder - just STEAM from its high water content blowing it up like a balloon. T3a: cooking the flour paste on the stove first gels the starch so it can hold lots of egg and water - and that water is the fuel for the steam. T3b: one dough, a whole family - eclairs, profiteroles, the cheese-puff gougere, the wheel-shaped Paris-Brest, the towering croquembouche.
topics.source: Grokipedia checked first (403); corroborated via Wikipedia 'Choux pastry' (pate a choux; boiled butter+water then flour cooked on stove gels the starch to hold more water, eggs beaten in after; high moisture -> steam puffs it into a hollow shell; products: eclair, profiterole, gougere, croquembouche, Paris-Brest).
topics.framing_note: Reveal the MECHANISM (steam-leavened, no yeast) and the breadth (one dough, many pastries). Scene-led/invert-wonder: lead with the HOLLOW interior as the puzzle, make steam the knowable answer. Prep-frame voice fine. ACCURACY RAIL: choux rises from steam alone - do NOT attribute its lift to yeast (that's croissant) or to baking powder. Dinner-test payoff = T2b (steam from its own water is the leavening). Keep the pastry-family rung as a recognition payoff, all four choices live.

topics.name: Confit and cassoulet
topics.scope: The southwest-French trick of cooking meat IN fat - to eat and to keep. T1: duck confit is duck legs cooked slowly and gently submerged in FAT - not fried, but poached in fat. T2a: it began as PRESERVATION - sealed under a cap of fat, meat keeps for months because oxygen can't reach it. T2b: confit comes from Gascony in southwest France, where cooks prize duck and goose fat the way others use olive oil. T3a: today 'confit' means anything cooked slow-and-low in fat - even garlic confit or tomato confit. T3b: cassoulet is the great bean-and-meat bake of the Languedoc - white beans slow-cooked with duck confit, sausage and pork. T4: cassoulet is named for the cassole, the earthenware pot it bakes in - the dish is named after its dish.
topics.source: Grokipedia checked first (403); corroborated via Wikipedia 'Confit' (duck/goose legs poached low in rendered fat ~<85-90C; fat seals from oxygen once cool = months of storage; specialty of southwest France/Occitania 'confit country'; generalized garlic/onion confit) and 'Cassoulet' (haricot beans + pork/sausage/duck-goose confit; Languedoc - Castelnaudary/Carcassonne/Toulouse; named after the cassole earthenware pot).
topics.framing_note: Reveal an ORIGIN + a preservation MECHANISM. Scene-led ('why cook a duck leg drowned in fat?'). Prep-frame + matter-of-fact meat wording is fine for a kid, never gory. ACCURACY RAIL: modern restaurant 'confit' is often just a cooking method with no preservation - distinguish that from the traditional keep-it-for-months purpose (the answer at T2a is the oxygen seal). Dinner-test payoff = T2a (the fat cap seals out air). Cassole-names-cassoulet is the vocab gem.

topics.name: Creme brulee and the custard
topics.scope: The dessert you crack with a spoon. T1: creme brulee's signature is the thin, glassy sugar crust you tap through - made by torching sugar on top until it caramelizes. T2a: the name means 'burnt cream' - the 'burnt' is that caramelized top. T2b: underneath is a custard - cream set with egg YOLKS (no flour) into a silky, wobbly base. T3a: custards bake in a water bath (bain-marie) so gentle, even heat sets them without scrambling the eggs or cracking. T3b: its cousin creme caramel (flan) hides its caramel at the BOTTOM - poured in first so it flips out as a sauce; creme brulee's caramel is torched on top and stays crisp.
topics.source: Grokipedia checked first (403); corroborated via Wikipedia 'Creme brulee' (custard of cream + egg yolks + sugar baked gently in a water bath; torched caramelized sugar crust on top; name = 'burnt cream'; earliest recipe Massialot 1691; distinct from creme caramel/flan where caramel lines the bottom).
topics.framing_note: Reveal a TECHNIQUE (gentle custard-setting) plus a caramelization payoff. Scene-led ('the dessert you crack'). Every answer is concrete (torched sugar, egg yolks, water bath, caramel-on-top vs bottom). ACCURACY RAIL: creme brulee's crust is torched ON TOP and crisp; flan's caramel is at the bottom and saucy - keep the two distinct. Dinner-test payoff = T3a (the bain-marie is WHY custards set smooth, not scrambled). Keep the flan contrast's answer live (caramel position).

topics.name: Croissant lamination and viennoiserie
topics.scope: The puzzle of how a croissant gets its hundred crackly layers. T1: a croissant's shattering flake comes from folding cold BUTTER into the dough over and over - not from special flour. T2a: each 'turn' (a fold in thirds) multiplies the sheets, building dozens of paper-thin alternating layers of dough and butter (numbers as context only). T2b: in the oven the WATER trapped in the butter flashes to steam and pries the layers apart, puffing them up. T3a: the butter must stay COLD and solid while you fold - if it warms and melts into the dough the layers merge and the pastry bakes dense, not flaky. T3b: unlike puff pastry, croissant dough also contains YEAST, so it rises from fermentation AND flakes from lamination - that's what makes it 'viennoiserie'. T4a: puff pastry (pate feuilletee) is the same lamination but with NO yeast - pure steam-lift, which is why a mille-feuille is crisp-shattery and a croissant is bready-flaky. T4b: the croissant isn't originally French - it descends from the Austrian crescent roll, the kipferl, carried to Paris in the 1800s (the buttery laminated version we know is early-1900s French). T5a: 'mille-feuille' literally means 'a thousand leaves' - the name IS the lamination trick in three words. T5b: you laminate by locking a flat block of butter inside the dough, then rolling and folding to spread it into sheets.
topics.source: Grokipedia checked first (403); corroborated via Wikipedia 'Croissant' (evolved from Austrian kipferl; August Zang's Paris Viennese bakery 1838-39; modern laminated butter croissant early 20th c.; yeast-leavened viennoiserie vs unleavened puff pastry; repeated butter-folding creates the layers) and 'Mille-feuille' (name = 'thousand leaves'). Build-stage ref: McGee (steam lift in lamination).
topics.framing_note: Technique flagship - reveal the MECHANISM (folded butter + steam) and the yeast-vs-none distinction. Scene-led ('why does a croissant SHATTER into flakes?'), never 'What is lamination?'. Prep-frame voice fine. ACCURACY RAIL: the croissant is Austrian-derived (kipferl), and the Marie-Antoinette-invented-the-croissant story is LEGEND - do not present it as fact. Dinner-test payoff = T2b (steam from the butter's water lifts the layers) and T3b (yeast is what separates croissant from puff pastry). Keep 'a thousand leaves' as a wonder-vocab gem, not a numbers question.

topics.name: Emulsion and hollandaise
topics.scope: The problem: fat and water refuse to mix, yet French cooking is full of sauces that hold them together. T1: a French vinaigrette (oil + vinegar) separates into layers the moment you stop shaking it - oil and water won't stay mixed on their own. T2: the fix is an emulsifier, a peace-broker molecule; in mayonnaise and hollandaise that job is done by EGG YOLK (context: the yolk compound lecithin grabs fat on one end and water on the other). T3: hollandaise is a WARM emulsion of egg yolk + melted butter + lemon; mayonnaise is its COLD cousin - egg yolk + oil, same trick. T4a: push it too hot or add the butter too fast and the sauce 'breaks' - it splits into a greasy, curdled puddle. T4b: the rescue is to start fresh with a NEW egg yolk (or a spoon of water) and slowly whisk the broken sauce back into it. T5a: swap hollandaise's lemon for a reduction of tarragon, shallot and vinegar and you get the classic steak sauce (bearnaise). T5b: beurre blanc holds butter and wine together with NO egg at all - the emulsion is carried by the butter's own milk solids and hard whisking.
topics.source: Grokipedia checked first (403 to automated fetch); corroborated via Wikipedia 'Hollandaise sauce' (egg-yolk lecithin emulsifies immiscible butter + lemon; breaks from excess heat; bearnaise = vinegar/shallot/tarragon/chervil reduction derivative; name = 'Dutch sauce'). Build-stage refs: McGee 'On Food and Cooking' (emulsion mechanism, breaking/repair), Escoffier 'Le Guide Culinaire'.
topics.framing_note: Mechanism flagship - the payoff is understanding WHY fat+water hold, not memorizing a recipe. Scene-led (the vinaigrette that re-separates). Keep 'lecithin' as CONTEXT/distractor only - the tested answer at T2 is 'egg yolk', never the molecule's name (banned-minutiae rule). ACCURACY RAIL: hollandaise is French despite meaning 'Dutch sauce' - don't attribute it to the Netherlands. Dinner-test payoff = T5b (beurre blanc emulsifies with NO egg) as the contrast that proves the concept, plus the practical T4b rescue. All four choices live: at the 'break' rung don't pre-name the cause in the stem.

topics.name: French kitchen words on a menu
topics.scope: The French phrases on a menu, each decoded to a real dish or technique (never a bare definition). T1: 'en croute' means the food is baked wrapped in PASTRY - like Beef Wellington. T2a: 'au gratin' means topped with cheese or breadcrumbs and browned under heat - like a bubbling potato gratin (from gratter, 'to scrape'). T2b: 'a la meuniere' means 'in the miller's-wife style' - the fish is dusted in FLOUR and pan-fried in butter (a la = 'in the style of'). T3a: 'flambe' means a splash of brandy or liqueur is set ALIGHT in the pan - the flame is the show, as in crepes Suzette. T3b: the belief that flambeing burns off ALL the alcohol is a myth - only about a quarter actually burns away, so most of it stays.
topics.source: Grokipedia checked first (403); corroborated via Wikipedia 'Beef Wellington' (en croute = 'in pastry'), 'Gratin' (browned cheese/breadcrumb crust; from gratter 'to scrape'; e.g. gratin dauphinois), 'Flambe' (ignited spirit ~40% ABV, ~one-quarter of alcohol burns off; crepes Suzette, cherries jubilee, bananas Foster; 'flamed'). Standard culinary usage for 'a la meuniere' (floured + butter-fried, e.g. sole meuniere).
topics.framing_note: Vocabulary ladder made FOOD-ANCHORED - every answer is a dish or a technique, never a dictionary gloss; scene-led ('what does en croute promise on a menu?'). ACCURACY RAIL (the payoff): flambeing does NOT burn off all the alcohol - only ~a quarter goes, most remains; correct the common myth. Dinner-test payoff = T3b (the alcohol mostly stays). Cover the two explicit seed terms (a la, en croute) plus au gratin and flambe. Keep all four choices live - don't let the stem restate the technique the term names.

topics.name: Ratatouille and Provence
topics.scope: The sun-drenched vegetable stew of southern France - and why it's younger than it looks. T1: ratatouille is a vegetable stew from Provence (around Nice) - eggplant, zucchini, peppers and onion all bound together with tomato. T2a: its Provencal flavor comes from herbes de Provence - thyme, rosemary, bay and the like. T2b: purists cook each vegetable SEPARATELY first, then combine, so each keeps its own texture instead of collapsing into mush. T3a: ratatouille could NOT have existed in old Provence - two of its anchors, tomatoes AND peppers, are New World crops that only reached Europe after Columbus. T3b: the neat fanned-out spiral from the movie isn't classic ratatouille - that's confit byaldi, thin slices baked in a pattern.
topics.source: Grokipedia checked first (403); corroborated via Wikipedia 'Ratatouille' (Provencal/Nicoise stew of tomato, onion, garlic, courgette, aubergine, pepper + Provencal herbs; purist method cooks vegetables separately then combines; no modern-form recipe before late-19th/early-20th c., ingredients arrived post-16th-c Columbian contact; confit byaldi = refined sliced version).
topics.framing_note: Reveal an ORIGIN + a Columbian-Exchange accuracy beat where the FOOD is the anchor. Scene-led ('the stew of a Provencal summer'). ACCURACY RAIL (the payoff): tomatoes and peppers are New World crops - a genuine 'old Provencal' ratatouille is impossible before ~1500, and the named dish is only ~a century old; never imply a medieval ratatouille. Dinner-test payoff = T3a (its two anchors are post-Columbian). Confit byaldi is the wonder gem. All four choices live.

topics.name: Stock, fond and mirepoix
topics.scope: The unglamorous pot of bones that classical French cooking is secretly built on. T1: real French cooking starts with a pot of bones and vegetables simmered for hours - the 'stock', whose French name FOND literally means 'foundation'. T2a: the trio of vegetables flavoring almost every French stock and braise is onion, carrot and celery - the mirepoix. T2b: stock gets its body - that lip-sticking richness - from collagen in the bones dissolving into GELATIN. T3a: white stock uses raw bones; brown stock ROASTS the bones first for deeper color and flavor. T3b: you SIMMER a stock, never hard-boil it - boiling churns fat and scum back in and turns it cloudy. T4: boil a brown stock way down and it concentrates into demi-glace, a syrupy, intense sauce base.
topics.source: Grokipedia checked first (403); corroborated via Wikipedia 'Stock (food)' (fond = foundation; fond blanc raw bones + mirepoix of onion/carrot/celery; fond brun = roasted bones; bone collagen -> gelatin gives body; simmer-not-boil for clarity; reduction to demi-glace). Build-stage ref: Escoffier 'Le Guide Culinaire' (stock as the base of all sauces).
topics.framing_note: Foundational technique ladder - reveal WHY stock matters (gelatin body, the base under sauces). Scene-led ('the pot French cooking is secretly built on'). Answers are concrete: the mirepoix trio, gelatin, roasted bones, simmer-not-boil, demi-glace - never a bare definition. ACCURACY RAIL: keep 'fond' meaning literal ('foundation') and don't confuse mirepoix (onion/carrot/celery) with the Cajun 'holy trinity' (onion/celery/bell pepper). Dinner-test payoff = T2b (collagen -> gelatin is what gives stock body). All choices live.

topics.name: The French omelette
topics.scope: The two-egg dish chefs use to judge each other - all technique, no browning. T1: a proper French omelette is pale YELLOW, never brown - browning means the pan was too hot. T2a: you keep the eggs moving constantly over gentle heat so the curd stays tiny, soft and creamy. T2b: the French leave the center slightly runny - they call it baveuse. T3a: it's rolled into a neat oval, not folded flat and stuffed like an American diner omelette (which is deliberately browned and filling-heavy). T3b: the world-famous omelette de la Mere Poulard at Mont-Saint-Michel is prized purely for TECHNIQUE - served plain, no fillings.
topics.source: Grokipedia checked first (403); corroborated via Wikipedia 'Omelette' (classic French: butter, gentle heat, constant early stirring, unbrowned, soft interior, rolled oval; American version cooked hotter, browned, folded flat, heavy fillings; omelette de la mere Poulard of Mont-Saint-Michel, 'most famous omelette', served plain).
topics.framing_note: Technique ladder - the wonder is that restraint (no browning, no fillings) is the mark of skill. Scene-led/invert: 'why is a browned omelette the sign of a WORSE cook?'. Prep-frame voice fine. ACCURACY RAIL: keep the French-vs-American contrast honest (pale/rolled/creamy vs browned/folded/stuffed) - neither is 'wrong', they're different dishes. Dinner-test payoff = T3a (rolled and pale, the French signature). 'Baveuse' is the vocab gem. All four choices live.

topics.name: The braise (boeuf bourguignon and coq au vin)
topics.scope: The counterintuitive truth that the cheapest, toughest cuts make the most tender, luxurious dishes - if you braise them. T1: a slow-cooked stew uses the TOUGH, cheap cuts (shoulder, chuck, shank), the opposite of a quick-grilled steak - and they come out meltingly tender. T2a: what braising melts is collagen, the chewy connective tissue, which long moist heat turns into silky gelatin. T2b: boeuf bourguignon is beef braised in RED wine (Burgundy) with a garnish of lardons, mushrooms and pearl onions - red wine is the braising liquid. T3a: coq au vin was invented to rescue an OLD ROOSTER - a bird too tough to roast, braised for hours in wine until tender (the name literally means 'rooster in wine'). T3b: lardons - little strips of cured pork fried to render their fat - build the savory base of both braises. T4a: you SEAR the meat brown first, before any liquid; the browned bits stuck to the pot (the fond) get scraped up by the wine to build deep flavor. T4b: as it cooks the wine doesn't mostly 'tenderize' - it REDUCES, concentrating into the body of the sauce. T5a: despite the name, boeuf BOURGUIGNON isn't an ancient Burgundy peasant dish - it first appears in 1860s Paris cooking; the 'Burgundy' really points to the WINE. T5b: the tale that coq au vin dates to Julius Caesar and the Gauls is just legend - the recipe isn't written down until the early 1900s.
topics.source: Grokipedia checked first (403); corroborated via Wikipedia 'Beef bourguignon' (tough collagen-rich cut braised in red Burgundy + stock; lardons/pearl onion/mushroom garnish; NOT originally a Burgundy regional dish, first documented 1867, Paris-bistro association) and 'Coq au vin' (old mature rooster needs slow braise; Gaul/Caesar origin is undocumented legend, recipe first documented early 20th c.). Build-stage ref: McGee (collagen-to-gelatin at braising temps).
topics.framing_note: Reveal the MECHANISM (collagen -> gelatin) through two flagship dishes; prep-frame voice ('you sear it, then braise it') is fine. Scene-led hook = 'why does a fancy braise start with the CHEAPEST meat?'. ACCURACY RAILS (two myth-busts baked in as payoffs): boeuf bourguignon is not an ancient Burgundian peasant recipe (label the Burgundy link as the WINE), and the coq au vin / Julius Caesar origin is LEGEND. Avoid overstating wine as a tenderizer - the answer is that it reduces into the sauce. Dinner-test payoff = T3a (the old rooster - the name's real reason). No bare human-name answers.

topics.name: The five mother sauces
topics.scope: The idea that almost every classic French sauce descends from a handful of 'mother' sauces, each = a liquid + a thickener. T1a: the creamy white sauce in lasagna and mac-and-cheese is milk thickened with a cooked flour-and-butter paste (bechamel). T1b: that flour-cooked-in-fat paste is the thickener under most classic sauces (a roux). T2a: loosen a pale roux with clear chicken or fish stock and you get the 'velvet' sauce (veloute) - stock is the liquid. T2b: cook the roux dark and add brown roasted-bone stock and you get the deep-brown mother sauce (espagnole). T3a: ONE mother sauce is thickened by its main ingredient cooking down, not by roux at all (tomato) - and it's the only one that couldn't exist in France before the Americas. T3b: the fifth mother sauce uses no roux and no long simmer - it's an emulsion held by egg yolk (hollandaise). T4a: stir grated cheese into bechamel and you get the sauce of a gratin (Mornay). T4b: add a tarragon-shallot-vinegar reduction to hollandaise and you get the classic steak sauce (bearnaise). T4c: Escoffier's famous five updated Careme's earlier list by promoting two sauces Careme hadn't ranked as 'mother' (tomato and hollandaise). T5a: the DARKER you cook a roux, the LESS it thickens - toasting breaks the starch, so a near-black gumbo roux is for flavor, not body. T5b: reduce espagnole with more brown stock and it concentrates into the glossy, intense sauce base pros prize (demi-glace).
topics.source: Grokipedia (grokipedia.com) checked first per source priority but returned HTTP 403 to automated fetch; corroborated via Wikipedia 'Mother sauce' (Careme 4 / Escoffier 5; per-sauce base + thickener table; bechamel=milk+white roux, veloute=clear stock+blond roux, espagnole=brown stock+brown roux, tomate=tomatoes, hollandaise=egg-yolk emulsion). Build-stage primary refs: Escoffier 'Le Guide Culinaire' (1903), McGee 'On Food and Cooking' (roux browning vs thickening power).
topics.framing_note: Keystone French ladder - reveal the SYSTEM (liquid + thickener) not a definition; scene-led ('the creamy sauce in lasagna...'), never 'What is a mother sauce?'. Every answer is a specific sauce, ingredient, or a mechanism fact - never a bare human name; the Careme-vs-Escoffier rung is answered by WHICH SAUCES (tomato/hollandaise) were added, not by the chefs' names. ACCURACY RAIL: tomato is a New World crop, so sauce tomate could only join the French canon AFTER the Columbian Exchange - never imply a medieval French tomato sauce. Dinner-test payoff = T5a (darker roux thickens LESS, the counterintuitive mechanism) and the pair that break the roux pattern (hollandaise=emulsion, tomato=fruit-thickened). Keep all four choices live: don't name the thickener the stem is asking for.

topics.name: The souffle
topics.scope: The dessert-or-dinner that dramatically rises tall then sinks. T1: a souffle's puff comes from air beaten into egg WHITES, gently folded into a flavored base. T2a: in the oven the trapped air expands and moisture turns to steam - together they inflate it and it rises tall. T2b: the name says it all - souffle is French for 'puffed / blown'. T3a: it ALWAYS collapses a few minutes after leaving the oven, because as it cools the air contracts and the structure sinks. T3b: a savory cheese souffle is built on a thick bechamel base, a sweet one on pastry cream or fruit - the base carries flavor, the whites carry the lift. T4: don't open the oven mid-bake - the rush of cool air can make it fall early.
topics.source: Grokipedia checked first (403); corroborated via Wikipedia 'Souffle' (beaten egg whites trap air; heat expands air + converts moisture to steam = rise; cooling contracts them = collapse in 5-10 min; name = past participle of souffler 'to blow/puff/inflate'; savory cheese/vegetable base vs sweet chocolate/fruit).
topics.framing_note: Mechanism ladder - the wonder is the rise-AND-fall. Scene-led ('why does it sink the moment it hits the table?'). Every answer is a concrete cause (beaten whites, expanding air + steam, cooling, the base). Link to the mother-sauce ladder via the bechamel base. ACCURACY RAIL: the collapse is normal physics (cooling contraction), not a 'failed' souffle - don't imply a droop means the cook erred. Dinner-test payoff = T3a (it falls because it cools). Keep all four choices live.

topics.name: Authentic ragu alla bolognese
topics.scope: The dish the world gets wrong.
