T4: a pile of sugar or white bread sends blood glucose up fast, triggering an insulin surge and a crash that leaves you hungry again within an hour — pairing carbs with protein, fat or fiber blunts the spike (that's why cereal alone leaves you starving mid-morning).
topics.source: Harvard Nutrition Source (Carbohydrates, Fiber, whole vs refined grains); NIH/NIDDK on glycemic response & insulin; gut-microbiome fiber-fermentation literature (short-chain fatty acids). Grokipedia attempted (403).
topics.framing_note: Scene-led; answers are the mechanism or the food part (fiber, bran+germ, gut bacteria). Dinner-test payoff: T3 (fiber feeds your gut bacteria, not you) — this quietly bridges to the fermentation strand. ACCURACY RAIL: whole-food lean is fine and settled here, but do NOT demonize all carbs — a whole potato, oats and fruit are good foods; the villain is the refined/empty version, not the macro. Settled physiology → vision_mandated false.

topics.name: Eating for energy vs growth vs recovery
topics.strand: Building a diet that fits your goals
topics.scope: The same foods, aimed at different jobs. T2 (scene): your body runs on two main fuels — carbs for fast, hard effort (a sprint) and fat for slow all-day endurance; a marathoner 'hits the wall' near mile 20 when the fast fuel runs out — the stored carbohydrate (glycogen) — and is forced down to fat-burning pace. T3 (growth): for building a body — a kid in a growth spurt, a healing broken bone — the key is protein plus enough total calories and bone minerals (calcium, and vitamin D to use it); under-eating stalls growth. T4 (recovery): after hard exercise, muscle rebuilds best when you eat protein (the leucine trigger from the protein ladder) fairly soon after, alongside carbs to reload the glycogen you burned. T5 (payoff, ties the strand): this is why one plate doesn't fit everyone — an endurance athlete carb-loads before a race, a growing teen needs extra protein and calories, a person sitting all day needs fewer carbs; the foods are the same, the ratios change with the goal.
topics.source: Sports-nutrition consensus (glycogen depletion / 'the wall'); Examine.com & pediatric sports-nutrition guidance (protein + calories for growth, calcium/vitamin D for bone); post-exercise protein+carb recovery literature. Grokipedia attempted (403).
topics.framing_note: Scene-led; answers are the fuel or nutrient tied to the goal (glycogen, protein+carbs, adjust-the-ratio). Dinner-test payoff: T2 (the marathoner's 'wall' is running out of stored carbohydrate). ACCURACY RAIL: the post-workout 'anabolic window' is looser than gym lore claims — say 'fairly soon,' not a strict 30-minute deadline. Settled sports nutrition → vision_mandated false; T5 sets up the capstone tailoring ladder.

topics.name: Fats — what they do, and the seed-oil debate
topics.strand: Building a diet that fits your goals
topics.scope: From 'fat is the enemy' to the real modern argument. T2: fat is not the enemy — your brain is mostly fat (by dry weight), and dietary fat is what lets you absorb vitamins A, D, E and K; a truly fat-free diet starves the brain and blocks those vitamins. T3: fats come in families you can tell apart by behavior — saturated fats stay solid on the counter (butter, tallow, coconut), monounsaturated pours but firms in the fridge (olive oil), polyunsaturated stays liquid (fish omega-3, seed-oil omega-6); the answer names a fat family from how it acts. T3b (technique payoff): chefs deep-fry in high-smoke-point fats (tallow, refined oils) and save fragile extra-virgin olive oil as a finishing drizzle, because heat past the smoke point wrecks a fat. T4: the body needs both omega-3 (fatty fish — salmon, sardines) and omega-6 (seed oils), but the modern diet runs roughly 15-17x more omega-6 than omega-3 when older diets were near 1:1 — the fix is more oily fish, not fat-phobia. T5 (the debate, no verdict): 'seed oils' (soybean, corn, canola) are industrially extracted and very high in omega-6 linoleic acid; traditional-foods critics argue repeated heating oxidizes these fragile fats into harmful compounds and favor butter/tallow/olive oil, while the American Heart Association points to trials where swapping saturated fat for these oils improved heart markers — the honest answer names the actual crux (processing + oxidation + omega-6 excess), not a winner.
topics.source: AHA 'No reason to avoid seed oils' (2024) & Presidential Advisory on dietary fats (Circulation); PMC6247292 (omega-6 controversies); ACS ChemMatters 'Seed Oils'; traditional-foods skeptic literature (oxidation/OXLAMs, omega-6:3 ratio); NIH ODS on fat-soluble vitamins. Grokipedia attempted (403).
topics.framing_note: Scene-led; answers are foods, fat families, or the crux of the argument. Dinner-test payoff: T5 (the seed-oil fight is really about oxidation + omega-6:3 balance + processing, NOT 'fat is bad'). ACCURACY RAILS: present the seed-oil question as GENUINELY contested — human RCTs favor PUFA for heart markers, so do NOT assert seed oils are 'proven toxic'; steel-man BOTH sides; the tested answer is always the mechanism/crux, never a policy verdict. 'Brain is 60% fat' = by dry weight — phrase carefully. Contested-debate topic → vision_mandated true.

topics.name: Food is information — tailoring the diet to your goal
topics.strand: Building a diet that fits your goals
topics.scope: Capstone: food is more than calories — it's signals your body reads. T3 (scene): 200 calories of eggs and 200 calories of soda do completely different things to your appetite — protein and fat trip fullness signals, while sugar spikes then crashes and leaves you hungry, so 'a calorie' isn't the same for hunger. T4 (payoff): the 'protein leverage' idea — your appetite hunts for a protein target, so when food is protein-poor (chips, soda) you keep eating and overshoot on total calories chasing the protein you need; protein-rich meals satisfy on fewer calories. T5 (the debate, no verdict): this sits inside a real argument — the mainstream 'energy balance' view says weight is mostly calories-in vs calories-out (a calorie is a calorie), while the challenger view says WHAT you eat shifts hormones (like insulin), hunger and how the body uses those calories; the honest answer names the actual crux — both camps agree calories matter, they disagree on whether food QUALITY changes appetite and metabolism enough to matter more.
topics.source: Wikipedia + PMC10475875 (Protein Leverage Hypothesis, Simpson & Raubenheimer); satiety-hormone literature (ghrelin, CCK, GLP-1 responses to protein vs carb); carbohydrate-insulin model vs energy-balance model debate. Grokipedia attempted (403).
topics.framing_note: Scene-led; the tested answer is a concept/crux, never a verdict. Dinner-test payoff: T4 (low-protein food makes you overeat because appetite chases protein). ACCURACY RAILS: steel-man BOTH the energy-balance and food-quality/insulin camps — do not declare a winner; protein-leverage is a well-supported hypothesis, not a proven law. This is the strand's capstone ('build a diet that fits YOUR goals') → contested framing, vision_mandated true.

topics.name: Hydration — water, electrolytes, and the myths
topics.strand: Building a diet that fits your goals
topics.scope: Where water really comes from and what sweat really costs you. T2 (invert): you don't get water only from the tap — about a fifth of your daily water comes from FOOD, and some 'solid' foods are almost entirely water (a cucumber is ~97% water; watermelon and oranges over 90%; even a steak is ~65%). T3 (myth-buster): the famous 'drink 8 glasses a day' rule has no science behind it — it traces to a misread 1945 report that recommended ~2.5 liters total and then noted most of that is already in your food. T4 (payoff): when you sweat hard you lose more than water — you lose salt, and sodium is the main electrolyte in sweat (roughly a gram per liter); chugging only plain water after heavy sweating can leave you low on sodium, which is why athletes reach for electrolytes, not just water.
topics.source: Harvard Health 'Using food to stay hydrated' (~20% from food); Tufts/Michigan Medicine debunking the 8x8 rule (1945 Food & Nutrition Board report); Precision Hydration + AHA on sweat sodium (~1 g/L) and electrolyte replacement. Grokipedia attempted (403).
topics.framing_note: Scene-led; answers are foods, the myth's real origin, or the missing electrolyte. Dinner-test payoff: T3 (the 8-glasses rule is a misread report — food already supplies much of it). ACCURACY RAIL: don't over-scare — the point is 'plain water isn't the whole story', not that water is dangerous; sodium-isn't-the-enemy fits the traditional lean and is well-supported. Settled/myth-busting → vision_mandated false.

topics.name: Nutrient density — liver, nature's multivitamin
topics.strand: Building a diet that fits your goals
topics.scope: The most nutrition per calorie, built around the champion food. T1: 'empty calories' means energy with almost no vitamins or minerals — a can of soda; contrast a boiled egg of similar calories that is packed with nutrients (the concept: nutrition-per-calorie, not just calories). T2 (invert the wonder): ounce for ounce the single most nutrient-dense common food is an organ most kids never touch and old cultures treated as sacred and fed to pregnant mothers — liver. T3: liver's headline nutrient is vitamin A in the ready-to-use form (retinol) — one small serving holds roughly a week's worth, which is why you eat liver about once a week, not daily. T4 (payoff): you can actually get TOO much of that vitamin — Arctic explorers who ate polar-bear (or husky) liver got violently ill from vitamin A poisoning; the Inuit knew to avoid it. T5: nutrient density is about absorbability, not just amount — liver's iron is heme iron the body grabs easily, while spinach's iron is non-heme and partly locked up by the plant's own oxalates, so a small piece of liver beats a big bowl of spinach for usable iron (busting the Popeye idea). Also: in an egg it's the YOLK, not the white, that carries the choline, fat-soluble vitamins and minerals.
topics.source: Nutrivore beef-liver nutrient profile; Healthline 'Why liver is a superfood'; NIH ODS Vitamin A (retinol, hypervitaminosis A); documented Arctic polar-bear-liver hypervitaminosis A cases; NIH ODS Iron (heme vs non-heme, oxalate inhibition). Grokipedia attempted (403).
topics.framing_note: Scene-led, matter-of-fact about offal (never gory). Dinner-test payoff: T4 (polar-bear liver poisons you — too much vitamin A). ACCURACY RAILS: (1) vitamin A toxicity is real — DO NOT strawman the mainstream caution; the correct message is 'liver weekly, not daily'. (2) The Popeye 'misplaced-decimal' origin story is itself an unverified legend — do NOT teach it as fact; the true point is spinach iron is non-heme and poorly absorbed. Leans traditional-foods (steer toward organ/animal foods), so vision_mandated true; steel-man the 'limit organ meat' view via the toxicity angle.

topics.name: Protein — the body's building blocks
topics.strand: Building a diet that fits your goals
topics.scope: Protein deepened from 'quick fuel' myth to the muscle-building signal. T1 (invert): your body can't stockpile protein the way it hoards fat — so it takes the protein you eat apart into smaller reusable units and rebuilds its own; those units are amino acids. T2: of the ~20 amino acids, 9 are 'essential' — the body genuinely cannot make them, so a food source must supply them or you run short. T3: a 'complete' protein has all nine essentials in good amounts — eggs, fish, meat and dairy do; most single plant foods are short one (rice is low in lysine, beans low in methionine), which is exactly why rice AND beans eaten together make a complete protein (they cover each other's gap). T4: growing kids and muscle-builders need MORE protein per pound of bodyweight than a sedentary adult — the famous 0.8 g/kg figure is a floor to avoid deficiency, not the target for building (athletes aim far higher); the tested idea is 'more for growth/training', not the number. T5 (payoff): one specific amino acid, leucine, is the 'GO' switch that tells muscle to start building — which is why leucine-rich foods like eggs and whey trigger more muscle-building than an equal gram-count of low-leucine plant protein.
topics.source: Examine.com Protein Intake Guide; Harvard Health 'How much protein do you need'; StrengthLog protein-by-age; HealthyChildren.org teen-athlete protein; PMC8147948 (child protein requirements); Wikipedia (essential amino acids, complementary proteins, leucine/mTOR). Grokipedia attempted (403).
topics.framing_note: Scene-led; answers are foods or the named nutrient (amino acids, leucine, rice+beans), never a definition shell. Dinner-test payoff: T3 (rice+beans complete each other) and T5 (leucine is the build-signal). ACCURACY RAIL: steel-man plant protein — the honest point is that plants CAN make a complete protein by combining, not that they're useless. The RDA number and 'mTOR' are context/distractors only, never the tested answer (banned minutiae).

topics.name: The Mediterranean pattern — and the detective story behind it
topics.strand: Building a diet that fits your goals
topics.scope: The most-praised traditional diet, and the science that made it famous. T2: the 'Mediterranean diet' everyone recommends is really a 1950s-60s peasant pattern from southern Italy, Greece and Crete — vegetables, beans, bread, fish, and the signature fat that defines it, olive oil, with little red meat or sugar (the answer is the olive oil). T3 (origin): it came from a real detective story — American scientist Ancel Keys noticed poor Mediterranean villagers had far LESS heart disease than well-fed Americans and launched the 'Seven Countries Study' to compare their diets; the finding was that the olive-oil-and-fish eaters had less heart disease than the steak-and-butter eaters. T4: its strength is the whole PATTERN, not one magic food — olive oil instead of butter, fish instead of red meat, and the part everyone forgets: piles of vegetables and legumes (plus daily walking and shared meals). T5 (contested): Keys' work also launched the 'saturated fat causes heart disease' idea that shaped 50 years of low-fat advice — a leap now heavily re-examined, since his study showed correlation, not proof, and his cohort selection is criticized; the diet pattern holds up, the anti-saturated-fat verdict is disputed.
topics.source: MDPI Rev Cardiovasc Med 2025 'Ancel Keys, the Mediterranean Diet, and the Seven Countries Study: A Review' (PMC12027923); SevenCountriesStudy.com; PubMed 29134858 (Keys legacy); ongoing saturated-fat-hypothesis critique literature. Grokipedia attempted (403).
topics.framing_note: Scene-led; keep the FOOD as the anchor (olive oil, fish, beans) and Keys as context — never make a bare human name the answer; T3's answer is the FINDING (villagers had less heart disease), not 'Ancel Keys'. Dinner-test payoff: T5 (the diet is well-supported but 'saturated fat is the villain' is contested). ACCURACY RAILS: no anachronism issue (mid-20th-c pattern, tomatoes fine); do NOT flip into 'Keys was a fraud' — that's the opposite strawman; steel-man both. Contested science on T5 → vision_mandated true.

topics.name: The balanced plate — what each part is DOING
topics.strand: Building a diet that fits your goals
topics.scope: The plate model isn't arbitrary decoration; each section has a mechanical job. T1: on a plate of protein + vegetables + a smart carb + fat, the part your body uses to BUILD and repair itself (muscle, skin, hair) is the protein — meat, eggs, beans (not the bread or the oil). T2 (invert the wonder): a big green salad with NO oil on it barely gives you some of its vitamins — because vitamins A, D, E and K are fat-soluble, and fat is the truck that carries them in; the answer is the drizzle of oil/fat. T3: vegetables get to fill HALF the plate because they are the lowest-calorie section — mostly water and fiber (a cucumber is ~97% water), so you can eat a big satisfying volume for very few calories. T4: the difference between a 'smart' carb (oats, beans, a whole potato) and an 'empty' one (candy, white bread) is fiber — the smart carb releases its energy slowly. T4b (one model's choice): Harvard's Healthy Eating Plate pointedly does NOT count the potato as a vegetable and swaps the milk glass for a water glass, because a plain potato behaves like a fast starch, not a leafy vegetable.
topics.source: Harvard T.H. Chan Nutrition Source (Healthy Eating Plate vs USDA MyPlate); Harvard Health 'Comparison of Healthy Eating Plate and MyPlate'; USDA MyPlate; NIH ODS fat-soluble vitamin fact sheets. Grokipedia attempted (403).
topics.framing_note: Scene-led, food-anchored: every answer is a specific food or a food's job, never 'what is a balanced diet?'. The dinner-test payoff is T2 — the oil on the salad is what unlocks the salad's vitamins. ACCURACY RAIL: present the plate as a useful DEFAULT, not a law; do NOT inherit Harvard's blanket 'avoid red meat' framing (it conflicts with this bank's traditional-foods lean) — treat the potato-as-starch and water-not-milk choices as ONE model's reasoning, not settled truth. Keep red meat and whole-fat dairy neutral-to-positive.

topics.name: The vitamin hunt — deficiency diseases and the foods that cured them
topics.strand: Building a diet that fits your goals
topics.scope: Keystone food-history thread: one deadly deficiency + the specific food that fixes it, per rung. T2 (scurvy): on months-long voyages sailors' gums bled, teeth loosened and old wounds reopened — scurvy killed more men than battle, and the cure was a food: citrus (oranges, lemons). T3: in 1747 naval surgeon James Lind ran one of history's first controlled experiments, giving scurvy patients six different remedies — only the pair fed oranges and lemons recovered. T4 (the twist): Britain later switched from lemons to LIMES (grown in its own colonies) and scurvy quietly crept back, because limes carry only about half the vitamin C and it degraded further in storage — the cure was accidentally weakened even as the nickname 'limey' stuck. T4b (beriberi): sailors and city-dwellers eating polished WHITE rice grew weak and paralyzed; the missing piece was the very part milling removed — the rice bran/husk (thiamine), and Japanese navy doctor Takaki beat it by adding barley, meat and vegetables. T5 (pellagra): the corn-eating American South was ravaged by pellagra (dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia, death), yet Mexicans eating even MORE corn stayed well — because they soak corn in lime/ash (nixtamalization), which unlocks the niacin bound inside the corn; the South skipped that step. T5b (goiter): swollen thyroid 'goiter' afflicted ~30% of the Great Lakes 'goiter belt' until a trace mineral was added to salt — iodine; within a decade of iodized salt (1924) it nearly vanished.
topics.source: Wikipedia + Britannica + Science History Institute (James Lind 1747/publ.1753, citrus, limey, lime<lemon vitamin C); Wikipedia Takaki Kanehiro + Atlas Obscura 'Killer Rice' + Nobel (Eijkman) for beriberi/thiamine; Wikipedia Pellagra & Nixtamalization + Goldberger history; Healio + J. Nutrition (David Marine) on iodized salt 1924 Michigan, ~30%→<2% goiter. Grokipedia attempted (403).
topics.framing_note: Scene-led, invert the wonder (lead with the deadly mystery, make the FOOD the knowable answer). One coherent theme (a deficiency + the food/food-process that cures it); the scientist is always context, never the answer. Dinner-test payoffs: T4 (limes were worse than lemons) and T5 (nixtamalization — soaking corn in lime unlocks niacin). ACCURACY RAILS: Lind 1747 (published 1753); Takaki's 1880s fix PREDATES the vitamin theory (don't credit him with discovering thiamine); nixtamalization is Mesoamerican (lime/wood-ash); iodized salt 1924, Michigan. Settled history/science → vision_mandated false.

topics.name: Ultra-processed food — why it makes you overeat
topics.strand: Building a diet that fits your goals
topics.scope: The modern 'empty calories' problem, with the landmark experiment as payoff. T3 (scene): 'ultra-processed' isn't just any processing (freezing peas, canning beans is fine) — it means industrial formulations built from ingredients you'd never keep in a kitchen (emulsifiers, dyes, protein isolates, flavor blends); given a can of beans, frozen peas, and a neon breakfast cereal, the ultra-processed one is the cereal. T4 (payoff): in a 2019 NIH experiment (Kevin Hall), people were fed meals matched for calories, sugar, fat, salt AND fiber — yet on the ultra-processed menu they ate about 500 extra calories a day and gained weight, on the minimally-processed one they lost it. T5: the leading explanation is that ultra-processed food is engineered to be eaten FAST and soft and calorie-dense, and low in the protein/fiber that signal fullness — so the gut's 'stop eating' hormones can't keep up (people ate the ultra-processed food many calories-per-minute faster).
topics.source: NIH news + Cell Metabolism 2019 (Hall et al., ad-libitum UPF RCT, ~+500 kcal/day, n=20); Chris van Tulleken 'Ultra-Processed People'; NOVA classification (Monteiro, Sao Paulo). Grokipedia attempted (403).
topics.framing_note: Scene-led; answers are a food (the cereal), the experiment's result, or the mechanism (engineered to bypass fullness). Dinner-test payoff: T4 (matched for everything, people STILL overate ~500 cal on ultra-processed food). ACCURACY RAILS: the 'ultra-processed' (NOVA) category is itself debated and fuzzy — some ultra-processed foods aren't harmful, and Hall 2019 was one small (n=20) but landmark trial; present the lean-skeptical view honestly, not as settled dogma. The exact 500 number is context, the concept is tested. Contested definition → vision_mandated true.

topics.name: Weston Price and the traditional-foods idea
topics.strand: Building a diet that fits your goals
topics.scope: The dentist who mapped what old diets did right. T2 (scene): in the 1930s a Cleveland dentist, Weston A. Price, traveled to isolated peoples — Swiss Alpine villages, Scottish islands, African tribes, Pacific islanders — and found that those eating their old traditional diets had near-perfect teeth and almost no cavities, until white flour and sugar arrived and their teeth began to rot (answer: their teeth decayed once modern flour/sugar came in). T3: the healthiest groups all prized certain 'sacred' foods rich in fat-soluble vitamins — organ meats, fish eggs, shellfish, and deep-yellow butter from cows on fast-growing spring grass. T4 (payoff): Price found a mystery nutrient in those foods, more powerful than vitamins A and D at building strong bones and teeth, and named it 'Activator X'; decades later (2007) it was identified as vitamin K2, which steers calcium into bones and teeth and away from arteries. T5: this is the root of the modern traditional-foods movement — fermented foods (sauerkraut, natto, yogurt), bone broth, whole-fat dairy, and soaked or soured grains; the honest caveat is Price's evidence was observational travel fieldwork, not controlled trials.
topics.source: Weston A. Price Foundation (Activator X = vitamin K2 MK-4, identified 2007 by Chris Masterjohn/Sally Fallon); Price, 'Nutrition and Physical Degeneration' (1939); Dr. Steven Lin 'Mystery of Activator X'; K2 physiology literature. Grokipedia attempted (403).
topics.framing_note: Scene-led; the FOODS are the anchor (spring butter, organ meats, natto, ferments) and Price is context. Dinner-test payoff: T4 (Activator X turned out to be vitamin K2). ACCURACY RAIL: be honest that Price's fieldwork was OBSERVATIONAL and some conclusions are debated — celebrate the core insight (whole traditional foods beat white-flour-and-sugar) without overclaiming. Traditional-foods advocacy → vision_mandated true; do not strawman mainstream nutrition.

strands.strand: Macros: why your body needs them

topics.name: Carbs are fuel: simple, complex & the glycogen battery
topics.strand: Macros: why your body needs them
topics.scope: Carbohydrates are the body's quick fuel — where they come from, fast vs slow, and how the body stores them. T1: nearly all carbs are built by PLANTS out of sunlight — bread, rice, potato, fruit, and sugar all trace back to a plant storing energy, so carbs are basically edible sunlight. T2: 'simple' carbs (the sugar in candy, juice, honey) are small and hit the blood fast; 'complex' carbs (the starch in bread, rice, potato) are long chains that break down slower — the difference between a sugar rush and steady energy. T3 (payoff): your body's ready fuel is glucose, and your BRAIN is the greediest customer — it runs almost entirely on glucose and burns a big share of your daily carbs just thinking. T4: extra carbs get packed away as GLYCOGEN — a fast-access battery stashed in your liver and muscles; a marathoner 'carb-loads' on a big pasta dinner the night before to top that battery off. T5: run the battery empty and you 'hit the wall' — the sudden mile-20 exhaustion when muscle glycogen runs out and the body scrambles to burn fat instead. Also seeds: fruit's sugar (fructose) is handled mainly by the liver; the body CAN run on fat/ketones when carbs are scarce, so carbs are the DEFAULT fuel, not the only one.
topics.source: Established physiology (glucose is the body's primary ready fuel; brain relies heavily on glucose, ~120 g/day; glycogen stored in liver + muscle; endurance carb-loading and glycogen depletion 'the wall'; fructose primarily hepatic; ketone/fat oxidation as alternative fuel). Build-stage cross-check: Grokipedia/Wikipedia 'Carbohydrate', 'Glycogen', 'Carbohydrate loading', 'Ketosis'. Grokipedia WebFetch 403 this session.
topics.framing_note: Reveal the MECHANISM (quick fuel + storage battery). Scene-led (a candy rush; a marathoner's pasta dinner; hitting the wall at mile 20), never 'What is a carbohydrate?'. Accuracy rail: do NOT claim carbs are strictly essential — the body can run on fat/ketones (nod to it so the low-carb view isn't strawmanned), so frame carbs as the READY/DEFAULT fuel; brain-runs-on-glucose (~120 g/day) taught as concept, never the number as the answer; glycogen taught as 'the carb battery', not biochem. Dinner-test payoff = the glycogen-battery / carb-loading rung. Settled mechanism, but keep the low-carb steel-man alive in the fruit/ketone rungs.

topics.name: Collagen & gelatin: the protein in bone broth
topics.strand: Macros: why your body needs them
topics.scope: The most abundant protein in your body is a stringy 'glue' called collagen — and it's the same stuff that makes a great broth wobble. T1: the tough, chewy connective tissue in a cheap cut, and the gristle around a joint, is collagen — the body's built-in glue and scaffolding for skin, tendon, and bone. T2 (payoff): simmer bones and tough cuts low-and-slow for hours and the collagen melts into gelatin — the reason a proper stock or bone broth sets to a jiggly jelly in the fridge, and the reason cheap tough cuts (shank, oxtail) turn meltingly tender when braised. T3: that same gelatin, purified, is what sets a wobbling jelly, a gummy candy, and panna cotta — a dessert built, surprisingly, from animal collagen.
topics.source: Established food science (collagen = most abundant body protein, connective tissue; heat converts collagen to gelatin, giving stock its set and braises their tenderness; gelatin sets jelly/gummies/panna cotta). Build-stage cross-check: Grokipedia/Wikipedia 'Collagen', 'Gelatin', 'Stock (food)'. Grokipedia WebFetch 403 this session.
topics.framing_note: Prep-frame welcome (you simmer, you braise). Reveal the MECHANISM: long slow heat converts collagen -> gelatin (tough becomes tender + the broth jiggles). Scene-led (a stock that wobbles cold, a gummy bear), never 'What is collagen?'. Accuracy rail: gelatin is DENATURED collagen from animal connective tissue — keep it matter-of-fact for a kid (it comes from skin/bone/gristle), never gory; do NOT claim eating collagen rebuilds your own collagen (that's contested marketing) — the tested facts are the COOKING transformation and the dessert set. Dinner-test payoff = the broth-turns-to-jelly rung.

topics.name: Fat carries the vitamins: why you butter your carrots
topics.strand: Macros: why your body needs them
topics.scope: A cooking rule with a hidden reason — some vitamins can't get into you without fat riding shotgun. T1: vitamins A, D, E and K are 'fat-soluble' — they dissolve in fat, not water, so a meal needs some fat present for your body to absorb them at all. T2 (payoff): the orange in a carrot is beta-carotene, which your body converts to vitamin A — but eaten raw and fat-free you absorb little; add butter or oil (glazed carrots, carrots in a stew) and absorption jumps. T3: the same trick powers a salad — a drizzle of olive oil over leafy greens and tomatoes lets you actually absorb their fat-soluble goodness, while a fat-free dressing wastes much of it. T4: it's why traditional cooks paired fat with vegetables on instinct — spinach with butter, tomatoes simmered in olive oil (the red pigment lycopene is absorbed far better cooked in oil). T5: the flip side — fat-soluble vitamins can be BANKED in your body fat for a rainy day (unlike vitamin C, which you must eat daily), so a fat-rich food like egg yolk or cod-liver oil stores up vitamins A and D.
topics.source: Established nutrition (fat-soluble vitamins A/D/E/K require dietary fat for absorption and are stored in body fat; beta-carotene -> vitamin A; carotenoid/lycopene absorption enhanced by fat and by cooking). Build-stage cross-check: Grokipedia/Wikipedia 'Fat-soluble vitamin', 'Beta-Carotene', 'Lycopene'. Grokipedia WebFetch 403 this session.
topics.framing_note: Prep-frame welcome (you butter, you drizzle, you simmer). Reveal the MECHANISM: fat is the CARRIER for A/D/E/K. Invert the wonder — stem sets up 'why grandma always put butter on the carrots', the answer is 'the vitamin needs fat to be absorbed.' Accuracy rail: fat-soluble vitamins are A, D, E, K (NOT C, which is water-soluble); beta-carotene->vitamin A and lycopene are the concrete examples — teach the concept, not the compound names as the tested answer. Dinner-test payoff = the buttered-carrots / beta-carotene rung. Settled science, not vision-mandated.

topics.name: Fat is not the enemy: what fat actually does
topics.strand: Macros: why your body needs them
topics.scope: Fat spent decades cast as the diet villain, but it does jobs no other macro can. T1: fat is the body's densest fuel — gram for gram it packs more than double the energy of sugar or protein, which is why a single spoon of oil is so calorie-rich and why body fat is our long-term battery. T2: every one of your cells is wrapped in a wall built of fat (the membrane) — no dietary fat, no cell walls; fat is STRUCTURE, not just fuel. T3: your BRAIN is roughly 60% fat, and the insulation sheathing your nerves is fatty — which is why fat matters most for the youngest, fastest-growing brains (breast milk is deliberately rich in fat for exactly this). T4 (payoff): cholesterol — the word people fear — is the raw material your body turns into hormones (the ones that drive growth and puberty) and into vitamin D from sunlight; you would die without it, and your own liver makes most of it. T5: fat also makes a meal SATISFYING and slows digestion — the reason a fatty meal keeps hunger away for hours while a fat-free snack leaves you hungry soon after. Also seeds: fat under the skin insulates and cushions organs; fat is where much of a dish's FLAVOR lives (fat carries taste and aroma).
topics.source: Established physiology/biochemistry (fat ~9 kcal/g vs ~4 for carb/protein; phospholipid cell membranes; brain ~60% fat by dry weight, myelin is lipid-rich; cholesterol is precursor to steroid hormones + vitamin D + bile, mostly endogenously synthesized; dietary fat slows gastric emptying/increases satiety). Build-stage cross-check: Grokipedia/Wikipedia 'Fat', 'Cholesterol', 'Cell membrane', 'Myelin'. Grokipedia WebFetch 403 this session.
topics.framing_note: STANCE ladder (vision-mandated): steel-man the low-fat orthodoxy honestly (there WERE reasons dietitians pushed low-fat) but LEAN toward 'fat is essential and was over-vilified.' Empowerment: a kid learns what fat DOES. Scene-led (a spoon of oil, the fatty brain, fat-rich breast milk), never 'What is fat?'. ONE job per rung — fuel, membranes, brain, hormones/cholesterol, satiety, flavor are distinct payoffs. Accuracy rail: cholesterol is a precursor to steroid hormones + vitamin D and is mostly liver-made — do not moralize it as 'bad'; energy density taught as 'more than double' carbs/protein, never the exact 9-vs-4 number as the answer. Dinner-test payoff = the cholesterol-makes-hormones rung.

topics.name: Omega-3 vs omega-6: the fish-and-seed-oil balance
topics.strand: Macros: why your body needs them
topics.scope: Two families of fat your body can't make and must eat — and why their BALANCE is argued over. T1: omega-3 and omega-6 are both 'essential' fats (the body cannot build them from scratch); the richest omega-3 comes from OILY FISH — salmon, sardines, mackerel — plus flax and walnuts. T2 (payoff): the most usable omega-3s (the brain-and-heart forms, EPA and DHA) come ready-made in fish and shellfish, while the plant form (in flax/chia/walnut) is a 'starter' your body converts only poorly — which is why 'eat oily fish' beats 'drink flax oil.' T3: omega-6 is everywhere and easy to get — it's the dominant fat in seed/vegetable oils, so anyone eating modern processed food gets plenty (arguably too much). T4: the debate — traditional diets ran roughly balanced between the two families, but modern seed-oil-heavy diets tilt hard toward omega-6; one camp argues this ratio drives inflammation, the mainstream counter argues total omega-3 intake matters more than the ratio. T5: the practical takeaway BOTH sides share — most people are simply short on omega-3, so the fix is more oily fish (or eggs and beef from pastured animals), not obsessing over a number.
topics.source: Search: omega-6/omega-3 (PMC8504498 and PMC7721408 on low omega-6/3 ratio; Eufic 'Do seed oils cause inflammation?' for the mainstream steel-man; thewholehealthpractice 'Seed Oils: Striking the Right Balance') confirming both essential, EPA/DHA (fish) vs ALA (plants) conversion is poor, modern ~10-20:1 omega-6:3 tilt, and the genuine ratio-vs-absolute-intake scientific dispute (incl. Jackson et al. 2024 skepticism of the ratio).
topics.framing_note: VISION-MANDATED contested debate — a flagship 'great nutrition debate' of this strand: present the ratio-matters camp AND the mainstream 'absolute omega-3 is what counts' camp FAIRLY; the shared conclusion (eat more oily fish) is the honest closer, never a strawman of either side. Scene-led (a fillet of salmon; a bottle of vegetable oil). Accuracy rail: both are essential fatty acids; EPA/DHA (fish, ready-made) vs ALA (plants, poorly converted) is the key mechanism — teach 'fish gives the usable kind', never the abbreviations as the tested answer; do NOT overclaim omega-6 is toxic. Dinner-test payoff = the fish-gives-the-usable-omega-3 rung.

topics.name: Pemmican: the fat-and-protein food with no carbs
topics.strand: Macros: why your body needs them
topics.scope: The original survival superfood proves fat + protein alone can power a body for months. T1: pemmican is dried meat pounded to a powder and mixed roughly half-and-half with rendered fat (sometimes studded with dried berries) — a dense, nearly indestructible food developed by the Plains peoples of North America. T2 (payoff): it's almost pure FAT and PROTEIN with essentially no carbs, yet fur-trade voyageurs and polar explorers lived and hauled loaded canoes on roughly a pound of it a day — living proof the body runs fine on fat-and-protein when it must. T3: because it's so dry and fat-sealed, pemmican keeps for years with no refrigeration — the reason it crossed oceans on expeditions long before the canned tin existed.
topics.source: Search: pemmican (Wikipedia 'Pemmican'; Britannica 'Pemmican'; Lewis & Clark 'Making Pemmican') confirming ~1:1 dried-meat-to-rendered-fat, optional dried berries, Cree 'pimihkan' = 'manufactured fat', Plains-peoples origin, voyageur/polar-expedition use ~1 lb/day, multi-year shelf stability.
topics.framing_note: Food-driven history where the FOOD is the anchor (Cree 'pimihkan' = manufactured fat). Reveal the amazing FACT: a carb-free food fueling extreme labor. Scene-led (a voyageur's daily ration; a polar sledge), never 'What is pemmican?'. Prep-frame fine (you pound, you render). Accuracy rail: Indigenous North American origin (Plains / Cree) — attribute correctly, never as a European invention; berries are optional and the only carb source. Keep butchery/rendering matter-of-fact, not gory. Dinner-test payoff = the no-carbs-yet-fueled-explorers rung. Ties the whole strand together (a food that IS the macros, stripped to two).

topics.name: Protein: the body's repair-and-build crew
topics.strand: Macros: why your body needs them
topics.scope: Protein is the body's building AND working material — the 'grow-and-fix' macro, revealed one job at a time. T1: the reason a plate pairs meat/eggs/fish as the 'building' food is that your body patches a scraped knee and grows new muscle out of PROTEIN. T2: the stringy fibers you pull apart in a chicken breast literally ARE bundled muscle protein — eating meat means eating another animal's muscle. T3: hair and fingernails are a tough protein (keratin) too — another reason 'eat your protein' isn't only about muscle. T4: protein isn't just structure — the spit that makes a plain cracker taste sweeter the longer you chew is doing it with an ENZYME, and every enzyme is a protein (your digestion tools are protein). T5: the antibodies that fight off a cold are proteins as well, which is why a sick kid still needs to eat (broth, eggs) to rebuild defenses. T5: your body takes the protein in a steak APART into ~20 small pieces called amino acids and restrings those same 'beads' into YOUR proteins. T5: nine of those amino-acid beads your body cannot make at all — 'essential' on a nutrition label means 'must arrive in food.' T8 (payoff): hemoglobin, the stuff that makes blood red and carries your oxygen, is a protein cradle built around an iron atom — so a beef steak helps build the very blood in your veins. Also seeds: protein keeps you full far longer than a sugary cereal (satiety); a burn or wound heals by laying down new protein.
topics.source: Established textbook nutrition/biochemistry (protein as structural + functional macro; ~20 amino acids, 9 essential for humans; enzymes and antibodies are proteins; hemoglobin = globin protein + heme iron). Corroborated in passing via the complementary-protein searches (Wikipedia 'Protein combining', 'Diet for a Small Planet'). Grokipedia 'Protein'/'Essential amino acid' attempted but WebFetch returned HTTP 403 this session — flag for build-stage cross-check against Grokipedia + Wikipedia 'Protein (nutrient)', 'Essential amino acid', 'Hemoglobin'.
topics.framing_note: Empowerment voice: a kid learns WHY the plate needs a protein. Scene-led (a scraped knee, a chewed cracker, a cold), never 'What is protein?'. ONE job per rung — muscle, keratin, enzymes, antibodies, amino-acid recycling, 'essential', blood are SEVEN different payoffs, not restatements of each other. Accuracy rail: nine essential amino acids for humans (do NOT say 'all 20 must come from food'); amino acids are the tested CONCEPT ('beads'), never their chemical/Latin names as the answer. Dinner-test payoff = the hemoglobin / steak-builds-your-blood rung.

topics.name: Red meat's hidden payload: heme iron & B12
topics.strand: Macros: why your body needs them
topics.scope: Beyond protein, red meat carries two things plants barely provide — the honest empowerment case for a growing kid. T1: red meat is loaded with iron, the mineral your blood needs to carry oxygen — the reason liver and red meat are the classic 'build-your-blood' foods. T2 (payoff): meat's iron is the 'heme' kind, tucked inside the same molecule that makes blood red, and your gut grabs it far more readily than the iron in spinach — Popeye's spinach iron is REAL iron, but the body absorbs only a small fraction of it. T3: a squeeze of lemon or a sliced tomato (vitamin C) at the meal boosts how much of the PLANT iron you actually absorb — a real cooking trick. T4: vitamin B12 — needed to build blood and nerves — is found almost ONLY in animal foods (meat, eggs, dairy, fish); it's the nutrient strict vegans must take as a supplement. T5: this is why traditional cultures prized organ meats and blood dishes (liver, black pudding) — the most nutrient-dense bites per mouthful.
topics.source: Established nutrition (heme vs non-heme iron bioavailability; vitamin C enhances non-heme absorption; B12 essentially only in animal foods — the classic vegan-supplement fact). Recommend build-stage Grokipedia/Wikipedia cross-check: 'Heme iron', 'Human iron metabolism', 'Vitamin B12'. Grokipedia WebFetch 403 this session; not separately web-verified beyond established consensus.
topics.framing_note: Empowerment, not moralizing: a kid learns WHY meat is nutritionally valuable. STEEL-MAN both sides at build — mainstream 'limit red meat' guidance is real and honest; the iron+B12 case is the traditional-foods counter. Do not strawman either camp. Scene-led (a steak, Popeye's spinach, a wedge of lemon on the plate). Accuracy rail: heme vs non-heme is about ABSORPTION (bioavailability), not that plant iron is 'fake'; vitamin C boosting non-heme iron is well established. Teach concepts, never mg figures as the answer. VISION-MANDATED: 'red meat is uniquely valuable' is a culturally contested stance. Dinner-test payoff = the heme-iron / Popeye rung.

topics.name: Solid, liquid & spoiling: saturated, mono, poly (and the trans-fat villain)
topics.strand: Macros: why your body needs them
topics.scope: Why some fats are solid at room temperature and some stay liquid — and which one to actually cook in. T1: saturated fats (butter, lard, beef tallow, coconut oil) are SOLID at room temperature because their molecules are straight and stack tight; the pourable oils (olive, seed oils) can't stack. T2: that same tight packing makes saturated fats STABLE under heat — the reason old-school deep-frying used lard/tallow and why coconut oil sits happily on a shelf. T3 (payoff): the delicate polyunsaturated fats in seed oils have 'kinks' that break down and oxidize (go rancid, throw off-flavors and byproducts) when heated hard — the case for searing in a stable fat and saving fragile oils for cold use; olive oil (monounsaturated) sits in the sturdy middle. T4: this shelf-life problem is exactly what food companies 'solved' by hydrogenation — forcing hydrogen into liquid oil to make it solid and shelf-stable, which gave us margarine and, in 1911, Crisco, from cheap vegetable oil. T5: but hydrogenation birthed TRANS fat — the one fat scientists broadly agree is genuinely harmful (it worsens cholesterol both directions), now banned from the US food supply. The irony closer: the engineered fat built to replace 'unhealthy' butter turned out worse than what it replaced.
topics.source: Search: trans fat (PMC8452362 'Demise of Artificial Trans Fat'; FDA PHO final determination pages; Wikipedia 'Trans fat', 'Trans fat regulation') confirming Crisco 1911, hydrogenation makes liquid oil solid/shelf-stable, US ban (GRAS revoked 2015, compliance 2018, final ~2020-2021). Fat structure (saturated stacks tight->solid+stable; PUFA oxidizes on heating; MUFA intermediate) is established lipid chemistry — build-stage cross-check Grokipedia/Wikipedia 'Saturated fat', 'Polyunsaturated fat', 'Hydrogenation'.
topics.framing_note: VISION-MANDATED cooking/seed-oil debate: steel-man the mainstream (polyunsaturated fats lower LDL in trials; seed oils are not proven toxic) but LEAN skeptical of HEATED seed oils and sympathetic to stable traditional fats for high-heat cooking. Reveal the MECHANISM (molecular straightness -> solid + heat-stable). Scene-led (butter vs oil at room temp; a smoking pan). Accuracy rail: Crisco = 1911 (margarine, ~1869, predates it — attribute correctly); trans fat is the SETTLED-harmful one — teach 'the engineered solid fat we banned', not the ban date as the answer. Keep NATURAL saturated fat (contested) distinct from ARTIFICIAL trans fat (settled bad). Dinner-test payoff = the seed-oil-oxidizes-when-heated rung; the trans-fat-irony rung is the closer.

topics.name: The complete protein: all nine blocks in one bite
topics.strand: Macros: why your body needs them
topics.scope: Why nutritionists call some foods 'complete' proteins, built scene-first. T1: 'complete' means a food carries ALL nine essential amino acids in usable amounts at once — and the foods that pull that off are the animal ones: meat, fish, eggs, milk. T2: most single plant foods are 'incomplete' — a bowl of plain rice is short on one bead (lysine), a scoop of beans short on another (methionine) — so no one of them covers all nine alone. T3 (payoff): the EGG is the protein gold standard — scientists literally score every other protein against egg white, because an egg has to hold everything needed to build a whole chick from scratch. T4: milk actually hides two proteins with different speeds — the curds (casein) digest slow, the watery whey fast, which is why 'whey' is the athlete's shake and casein the 'overnight' one. T5: soy and quinoa are the rare PLANT foods complete on their own — the exceptions that prove the rule.
topics.source: Search: complementary/complete protein (Wikipedia 'Protein combining'; 'Diet for a Small Planet'; Forks Over Knives 'Myth of Complementary Protein'). Egg biological-value 'reference protein' and casein/whey digestion speeds are established food-science facts (recommend Grokipedia/Wikipedia 'Egg white', 'Biological value', 'Whey protein' cross-check at build). Grokipedia WebFetch 403 this session.
topics.framing_note: Invert the wonder: put 'the food scientists measure every other protein against' in the STEM, make the knowable EGG the answer. Scene-led, never 'What is a complete protein?'. Keep all four choices live (other complete animal foods as distractors, not obvious wrongs). Accuracy rail: NINE essential amino acids; egg is the reference protein — teach the CONCEPT 'gold-standard/reference protein', never a memorized biological-value number as the answer. Traditional-foods lean is gentle (animal foods happen to be complete) but the tested FACTS are settled, so not vision-mandated. Dinner-test payoff = the egg-is-the-reference rung.

topics.name: Whole vs refined grain: what's hidden in the bran
topics.strand: Macros: why your body needs them
topics.scope: A grain of wheat or rice has three parts, and refining throws two of them away. T1: a whole grain has a fibrous outer BRAN, a nutrient-packed GERM (the baby-plant embryo), and a big starchy ENDOSPERM (the energy store) — brown rice and whole-wheat flour keep all three. T2 (payoff): milling to make WHITE rice or WHITE flour strips off the bran and germ, leaving mostly the starchy endosperm — whiter, fluffier, longer-lasting on the shelf, but with the fiber and most nutrients removed. T3: history's hard lesson — when late-1800s mills began polishing rice bright white, whole regions of Asia came down with beriberi, a nerve-and-heart disease, because the vital nutrient lived in the discarded bran; switching back to unpolished rice cured it. T4: that's why white flour and rice are now 'enriched' — a few vitamins are sprayed back in to replace what milling removed, though the fiber never returns. T5: stone-ground and sourdough whole-grain breads keep more of the intact grain — part of why a dense traditional loaf eats so differently from a fluffy white supermarket one.
topics.source: Search: beriberi (Wikipedia 'Thiamine deficiency'; Nobelprize.org Eijkman; ScienceDirect 'Christiaan Eijkman') confirming polished/white rice removes the thiamine-rich bran, late-19th-c. milling change, Takaki (1880s Japanese Navy) and Eijkman (1897) work, cure via unpolished rice, and modern enrichment. Bran/germ/endosperm anatomy and refining trade-offs are established food science (build-stage cross-check: Grokipedia/Wikipedia 'Whole grain', 'Bran', 'Cereal germ').
topics.framing_note: Traditional-foods lean fits (whole grain vs stripped-white). Reveal the MECHANISM (bran/germ/endosperm; milling discards the good parts). Scene-led (brown vs white rice; a sack of white flour; a navy/village falling ill). Accuracy rail: beriberi = thiamine (B1) deficiency from POLISHED rice, late-1800s milling era — teach the STORY (the nutrient was in the discarded bran; unpolished rice cured it), never 'thiamine' or a scientist's name as the tested answer; enrichment adds some vitamins back but NOT fiber. Dinner-test payoff = the white-rice / beriberi rung. Settled.

topics.name: Why a growing kid and an athlete need more protein
topics.strand: Macros: why your body needs them
topics.scope: Protein need isn't one-size-fits-all — bodies that are BUILDING need more. T1: a growing kid is literally adding new body every year — bone, muscle, organs, all built from protein — so per pound of bodyweight a kid needs more than a sedentary grown-up. T2: lifting weights or hard training TEARS tiny bits of muscle; it grows back bigger only if protein is on hand to rebuild it — the 'eat protein after training' rule. T3 (payoff): among the amino-acid beads, one called leucine (rich in eggs, meat, dairy) acts as the 'GO' signal that switches muscle-building on — which is why athletes chase protein at breakfast, not just at dinner. T4: pregnant and nursing mothers need extra protein because they're building a whole second person. T5: the deficiency picture — kwashiorkor, the swollen-belly malnutrition seen when a just-weaned toddler is filled up on starchy porridge but given almost no protein; the name is a Ghanaian (Ga) word for 'the sickness the older child gets when the new baby comes.'
topics.source: Search: kwashiorkor (Wikipedia 'Kwashiorkor'; ScienceDirect overview; ResearchGate 'The Story of Kwashiorkor') confirming protein-deficiency-with-adequate-calories, Ga-language etymology 'deposed/displaced child', first described by Cicely Williams (1933, Gold Coast). Growth/athlete protein need and leucine as MPS trigger are established sports-nutrition facts (build-stage cross-check: Grokipedia/Wikipedia 'Leucine', 'Muscle protein synthesis').
topics.framing_note: Voice: honest and empowering — enough CALORIES is not the same as enough PROTEIN (that's the kwashiorkor lesson, and why the belly swells even when the child is 'fed'). Scene-led (a growing kid outgrowing shoes, post-workout, a bowl of porridge). Accuracy rail: kwashiorkor = protein deficiency WITH roughly adequate calories; Ga-language Ghanaian etymology; teach it as the vivid concept, never as a tested medical term or the discoverer's name as the answer. Leucine = 'the go-signal bead', concept not chemistry. Dinner-test payoff = the leucine / protein-timing rung.

strands.strand: Micros: vitamins & where you get them

topics.name: B12: the animal-only vitamin & why vegans supplement
topics.strand: Micros: vitamins & where you get them
topics.scope: The hook: the one nutrient a whole-foods plant diet simply cannot supply. T1: vitamin B12 keeps nerves and red blood cells healthy, and it lives in meat, fish, eggs and dairy — essentially NOT in plant foods. T2: the richest sources by far are liver and shellfish (clams). T3: the twist — B12 isn't made by animals OR plants, it's made by BACTERIA; animals bank it from microbes, which is why it ends up only in animal tissue. T3: that's why strict vegans must take a B12 supplement or fortified foods — a plants-only diet has no reliable source, and deficiency creeps in over years because the liver stores a big reserve. T4: even with plenty in the diet some people can't absorb it — the stomach must make 'intrinsic factor' to ferry B12 across the gut; without it you get pernicious anemia. T4 (payoff): the honest steel-man — a well-planned vegan diet CAN be healthy IF B12 is supplemented, but B12 is the clearest case where a plants-only diet cannot be sourced from whole foods alone.
topics.source: Britannica 'vitamin B12' (bacterial synthesis; liver/viscera richest; vegans risk deficiency without supplements/fortified foods). NCBI StatPearls NBK441923 (intrinsic factor, pernicious anemia, ~3-year vegan-diet deficiency onset). Corroborated across both.
topics.framing_note: Scene-led (the strict-vegan plate missing one thing), food-anchored answers. RAIL: B12 is made by BACTERIA, not synthesized by the animal itself; deficiency is slow because of liver stores. STANCE — steel-man both sides genuinely: supplemented vegan diets work fine, do NOT strawman vegans, but state honestly that B12 is the non-negotiable animal-food gap. Dinner-test payoff = the T4 steel-man rung. vision_mandated because it engages the vegan-diet debate.

topics.name: Calcium: dairy, greens & why spinach lies
topics.strand: Micros: vitamins & where you get them
topics.scope: The hook: two greens list the same calcium, but one hands almost none over. T1: calcium builds bones and teeth and fires muscles; the classic source is dairy — milk, cheese, yogurt. T2: plants supply it too — leafy greens like kale, collards, bok choy and broccoli. T3: but greens aren't equal — spinach LOOKS calcium-rich yet its oxalates lock most of it up, so you absorb far more from kale or collards than from the same spinach. T3: a sneaky top source is canned sardines and salmon — the tiny soft bones (softened by canning) are almost pure calcium, eaten without noticing. T4: calcium needs vitamin D to be absorbed at all — the link between the 'sunshine vitamin' and strong bones, and why they're paired in fortified milk. T4 (payoff): the smartest calcium foods carry their own helpers — canned sardines deliver calcium PLUS vitamin D PLUS fat in one bite, an all-in-one bone package.
topics.source: PMC8746734 (calcium bioavailability / food-matrix effects; spinach ~5% absorbed due to oxalate vs low-oxalate greens). AlgaeCal & Kaplan Clinic (spinach oxalate binding; kale/collards higher usable calcium). Hancock Health (non-dairy sources; canned sardine/salmon soft-bone calcium). Consistent across sources.
topics.framing_note: Scene-led (the spinach that looks like a calcium hero and isn't), food-anchored answers. RAIL: spinach calcium is bound by OXALATE so poorly absorbed — kale/collards win; calcium needs vitamin D to be absorbed. Settled science → vision_mandated:false. Dinner-test payoff = the canned-sardine-bones rung (the all-in-one calcium+D+fat package).

topics.name: Fat-soluble vitamins need fat (eat the butter with the veg)
topics.strand: Micros: vitamins & where you get them
topics.scope: The hook: you can eat the vitamin and still not absorb a bit of it. T1: some vitamins dissolve in water (C and the B's), and four dissolve only in FAT — the fat-soluble crew is A, D, E, K. T2: because they ride in fat, a fat-FREE meal wastes them — a dry salad of carrots and greens with zero fat lets much of the vitamin A pass straight through. T3: the fix is delicious — add oil, butter, cheese, avocado or a little meat and absorption jumps; olive-oil dressing isn't just flavor, it unlocks the nutrients. T3: mechanism — dietary fat triggers bile, which packages the vitamins into tiny droplets (micelles) the gut wall can take up; no fat, no carrier. T4: this is a real strike against the fat-free fad — skim milk and fat-free dressing can strand the fat-soluble vitamins, while whole milk and full-fat dressing absorb better. T4: unlike water-soluble vitamins (excess peed out daily), fat-soluble ones are STORED in the liver and body fat — you don't need them every day, but you CAN overdose (the polar-bear-liver vitamin A). T5 (payoff): the old-fashioned pairing was right — butter on the vegetables, oil on the salad, cheese with the broccoli; 'eat the butter with the veg' is smart nutrition, not a guilty indulgence.
topics.source: NCBI Bookshelf NBK234920 (Fat-Soluble Vitamins, RDA — micelle/bile absorption, storage) and PMC11242131 (A/D/E/K clinical review) consulted. ScienceDirect randomized crossover trial on dietary fat & carotenoid absorption (consulted: adding fat raises carotenoid uptake; absorption drops sharply below ~5g fat/meal). Water- vs fat-soluble storage/excretion: standard consensus.
topics.framing_note: Scene-led (the dry salad that wastes its own vitamins), food-anchored answers only. RAIL: the mnemonic is A/D/E/K; fat-soluble are STORED and can build up (contrast water-soluble excreted). LEAN (steel-man both): the absorption mechanism is settled science, but the payoff pushes against low-fat orthodoxy toward whole/traditional fats — present the low-fat side fairly, then the pairing case. Dinner-test payoff = the 'eat the butter with the veg' rung. vision_mandated for the fat-orthodoxy lean.

topics.name: Folate: the leaf vitamin
topics.strand: Micros: vitamins & where you get them
topics.scope: The hook: a vitamin literally named after leaves. T1: folate (vitamin B9) takes its name from the Latin folium, 'leaf,' because it was first pulled from leafy greens like spinach. T2: the best food sources are dark leafy greens, legumes (beans, lentils) and — again — liver. T3: folate is vital in early pregnancy — too little causes neural-tube defects like spina bifida, where the baby's spine doesn't close properly. T3: because that happens in the first weeks, often before a woman knows she's pregnant, many countries add folic acid to flour and bread by law, and birth defects dropped sharply. T4 (payoff): heat and water are folate's enemies — boiling greens leaches and destroys much of it, so raw or lightly-steamed greens keep more; the leaf vitamin is a fragile one.
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folate and Fill Your Plate 'The Discovery of the Vitamin Folate' (consulted: folium='leaf', first isolated from spinach 1941 by Mitchell/Snell/Williams; Lucy Wills 1931 pregnancy anemia). Codeage folate history + NTD fortification data. Corroborated.
topics.framing_note: Invert the wonder — put the 'named after a plant part' hook in the stem, answer is the leaf/food fact; never 'What is folate?'. RAIL: folium = 'leaf'; neural-tube defects form in the first weeks (why folate matters BEFORE and at conception, not just during). Settled → vision_mandated:false. Dinner-test payoff = the T4 fragility rung (boiling destroys folate, eat greens raw/steamed).

topics.name: Iodine: iodized salt & the end of the goiter belt
topics.strand: Micros: vitamins & where you get them
topics.scope: The hook: a swollen neck that vanished when they changed one thing in the salt shaker. T1: the thyroid gland needs iodine to work; without it the thyroid swells into a big neck lump — a goiter. T2: iodine comes from the SEA — fish, shellfish and especially seaweed are loaded, while people far inland often fell short. T3: whole inland regions were 'goiter belts' — the US Great Lakes/Midwest and the Swiss Alps had iodine-poor soil; in 1920s Michigan, 70-100% of schoolchildren in some areas had goiters. T3: the fix (1924, Michigan) was brilliantly cheap — add a trace of iodine to ordinary table SALT, since everyone already eats salt. T4 (payoff): it did more than shrink goiters — iodine deficiency in pregnancy stunts a child's brain, so iodized salt quietly RAISED average intelligence in the deficient regions. T4: severe deficiency in infancy caused cretinism (stunted growth and mental disability) — a great preventable harm erased by the right pinch of salt.
topics.source: Healio 'Iodized salt: centennial' and Michigan Public 'goiter belt' (consulted: iodine-poor upper-Midwest soil; 1920s 70-100% schoolchild goiter rates; 1924 Michigan iodized salt, Morton national rollout; Michigan goiter ~30%→<2% in a decade). PMC6919660 (cognitive effects of US salt iodization). Washington Post 100-years piece. Corroborated.
topics.framing_note: Scene-led (the neck lump / the schoolroom full of goiters), food-anchored answers (salt, seafood, seaweed). RAIL: iodine comes from the SEA (inland soil is poor); the intervention is iodized TABLE SALT, 1924 Michigan; deficiency in pregnancy/infancy harms the brain (cretinism). Settled → vision_mandated:false. Dinner-test payoff = the T4 rung (iodized salt raised children's intelligence).

topics.name: Iron: heme (meat) vs non-heme (plants)
topics.strand: Micros: vitamins & where you get them
topics.scope: The hook: two foods list the same iron on the label, but your body pulls far more from one. T1: iron lets red blood cells carry oxygen; run low and you get anemia (tired, pale, cold); red meat is the classic iron food. T2: there are two kinds — HEME iron (from meat and blood, the animal kind) which the body absorbs easily, and NON-HEME iron (from beans, lentils, spinach) which it absorbs poorly. T3: vitamin C dramatically boosts the weak plant iron — squeeze lemon on the lentils, eat peppers with the beans. T3: tannins in tea and coffee, and phytates in whole grains, BLOCK iron — a cup of tea with dinner cuts how much you absorb. T4: spinach's iron-powerhouse reputation is overrated — it has iron but oxalates bind it, so little gets in (Popeye is legend, not nutrition). T4: cooking acidic food like tomato sauce in a CAST-IRON pan leaches real, usable (non-heme) iron into the food. T5 (payoff): this is the honest core of 'why a kid needs some red meat' — heme iron from meat is the one reliably well-absorbed source, which is why iron-deficiency is more common in those who eat none, and why plant-iron eaters must lean on the vitamin-C trick.
topics.source: PubMed 11124756 (ascorbic acid enhances non-heme iron absorption; ~67% boost at 100mg vitamin C in single meals). Cast-iron leaching (~up to 16%, acidic/moist/long-cooked foods, non-heme form): appetise.io and WhatsCookingAmerica (consulted). Heme vs non-heme absorption ranges + tannin/phytate inhibition + spinach oxalate: standard nutrition consensus.
topics.framing_note: Scene-led (two dinners, one gives you the iron) and food-anchored; invert with the label-vs-absorption puzzle. RAIL: spinach iron is poorly absorbed (Popeye = legend); cast iron adds the NON-heme form. Steel-man both sides — plant-iron diets work WITH vitamin C pairing, don't strawman vegetarians — but state the honest asymmetry (heme absorbs best). Dinner-test payoff = the heme-iron 'why red meat' rung. vision_mandated because the payoff makes the bank's traditional-foods dietary claim.

topics.name: Niacin, pellagra & why corn must be nixtamalized
topics.strand: Micros: vitamins & where you get them
topics.scope: The hook: a people living on corn get a disease of the skin and the mind — and an ancient soaking trick was the cure all along. T1: a near corn-only diet brings PELLAGRA, the 'four D's' — dermatitis (sun-scorched skin), diarrhea, dementia, death. T2: the missing nutrient is niacin (vitamin B3); corn actually HAS niacin but locked in a form the body can't unlock, and corn is low in tryptophan (which the body can turn into niacin). T3: Mesoamericans solved it thousands of years ago by NIXTAMALIZATION — soaking dried corn in alkaline limewater or wood-ash water before grinding. T3: the alkali releases the bound niacin AND turns the corn into masa, the dough for tortillas and tamales — so those cultures ate corn for millennia with no pellagra. T4: when corn spread to Europe and the American South WITHOUT the soaking step (they took the crop, not the technique), pellagra epidemics exploded across the early-1900s US South. T4: Dr. Joseph Goldberger proved pellagra was DIETARY, not a germ — he showed adding meat, milk and eggs cured it. T5 (payoff): the true villain was a monotonous poverty diet, not corn itself — niacin-rich meat, milk, eggs and fish prevent pellagra, and the indigenous soaking wisdom beat the 'modern' corn-only diet. T5: that same alkaline treatment is what gives a corn tortilla and tortilla chips their distinctive flavor.
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pellagra and /Nixtamalization (consulted: bound niacin/niacytin, low tryptophan, calcium-hydroxide limewater NOT the fruit, tryptophan→niacin, US South epidemic, Goldberger). Southern Foodways Alliance 'Malnourished' + New World Encyclopedia Pellagra (Goldberger, spring sickness, indigenous immunity). Corroborates strongly across sources.
topics.framing_note: Scene-led (the corn-eating village falling ill / the ancient soaking pot), never 'What is niacin?'; the answer is always a food or food-history fact. CRITICAL RAIL: the 'lime' in limewater is CALCIUM HYDROXIDE (alkali), NOT the citrus fruit — a build must never confuse them; nixtamalization is pre-Columbian Mesoamerican; pellagra is a DEFICIENCY, not a contagion (Goldberger's whole point). Dinner-test payoff = Goldberger proving diet-not-germ / traditional wisdom beat the modern mono-diet.

topics.name: Thiamine & beriberi: how polishing rice white made people sick
topics.strand: Micros: vitamins & where you get them
topics.scope: The hook: making rice prettier and whiter set off an epidemic. T1: when Asian diets switched to polished WHITE rice, a crippling disease spread — beriberi (nerve damage, weakness, swelling, heart failure). T2: the missing nutrient is thiamine (vitamin B1), which lives in the rice's bran and germ — the exact outer layers polishing scrapes off to make rice white. T3: Christiaan Eijkman noticed hospital chickens fed leftover polished rice developed a beriberi-like paralysis and recovered when the bran was put back — an accidental clue that a MISSING food factor, not a germ, caused disease. T3: in the Japanese Navy, Kanehiro Takaki slashed beriberi by replacing white-rice rations with barley, meat, fish and vegetables — a diet fix decades before anyone knew what a vitamin was. T4 (payoff): beriberi, alongside scurvy and pellagra, helped BIRTH the very idea of a 'vitamin' — that food holds tiny essential factors whose ABSENCE causes disease. T4: the lesson still holds — over-refining a whole grain strips nutrients, and brown rice keeps the thiamine that white rice throws away.
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thiamine_deficiency and /Takaki_Kanehiro (consulted). The Hospitalist 'History of a Vitamin' and Atlas Obscura 'How Killer Rice Crippled Tokyo and the Japanese Navy' (Eijkman's chickens 1897; Takaki's Navy diet reform eliminating beriberi within years; bran contains thiamine). Corroborated.
topics.framing_note: Scene-led (the whiter rice that sickened a navy), answers are food/food-history facts. RAIL: thiamine sits in the BRAN/GERM removed by polishing; Eijkman's chicken finding was an accidental clue and Takaki fixed it by diet BEFORE the 'vitamin' concept existed — don't credit them with knowing the molecule. Lightly supports the anti-over-refined lean but is settled history → vision_mandated:false. Dinner-test payoff = the T4 'birth of the vitamin idea' rung.

topics.name: Variety beats any single superfood
topics.strand: Micros: vitamins & where you get them
topics.scope: The hook: every 'miracle food' is missing something. T2: no single food is complete — the body needs dozens of different nutrients that no one ingredient supplies, so any lone 'superfood' leaves a gap. T3: the proof is written in disease — scurvy, beriberi, pellagra and goiter were every one a disease of MONOTONY (citrus-less voyages, white rice, corn-only, no seafood); variety is the oldest cure. T3: 'eat the rainbow' is real nutrition, not a slogan — different colors are different protective compounds: orange = carotene, red tomato = lycopene, purple = anthocyanins, deep green = folate and vitamin K. T4 (payoff): the honest steel-man — 'superfoods' like blueberries and kale genuinely are nutritious; the error is the MARKETING that sells one food (or one pill) as a shortcut. Whole-food variety, not a hero ingredient, is what actually works.
topics.source: Synthesizes the verified deficiency-disease ladders in this sub-strand (scurvy=vitamin C, beriberi=thiamine, pellagra=niacin, goiter=iodine — each corroborated above). 'Eat the rainbow' phytonutrient color→compound mapping (carotene/lycopene/anthocyanin) and superfood-marketing critique: standard nutrition consensus.
topics.framing_note: Scene-led (the marketed 'miracle food' that can't stand alone), food-anchored answers (name the color's compound, name the monotony disease). RAIL: do NOT strawman — superfoods ARE nutritious; the target is the SHORTCUT claim, not the food. LEAN (steel-man both): mainstream 'balanced diet' and the traditional whole-food-variety view converge here against reductionist single-food/pill marketing. vision_mandated:true (nutrition-stance topic). Dinner-test payoff = the T4 superfood steel-man rung.

topics.name: Vitamin A: liver, orange veg & the carrot myth
topics.strand: Micros: vitamins & where you get them
topics.scope: The hook: the propaganda story that carrots give you night vision, and the food that really is a vitamin-A bomb. T1: vitamin A powers dim-light sight (real deficiency causes night blindness) and the single richest food source is LIVER — a small piece packs a huge dose. T2: orange and dark-green veg (carrots, sweet potato, pumpkin, spinach, kale) supply it as BETA-CAROTENE, the orange pigment the body converts to vitamin A. T2: egg yolks, butter and whole milk carry ready-made vitamin A (retinol) — the fat is why. T3: the 'carrots for super night vision' claim is HALF-true — fixing a deficiency restores normal night sight, but extra carrots past adequacy give no superpower. T3 (history): the myth was WWII British propaganda — the RAF credited ace John 'Cat's Eyes' Cunningham's carrot habit for his night kills to HIDE that pilots were using secret airborne radar. T4: plant beta-carotene is self-limiting (the body converts only what it needs, so you can't poison yourself — though enough turns skin orange, carotenemia); animal retinol is NOT capped. T4: because retinol isn't capped, some animal liver is TOO rich — polar-bear and seal liver hold such concentrated vitamin A that eating them poisons a person (headache, peeling skin). T5 (payoff): in 1913 Antarctic explorers Mawson and Mertz, starving, ate their sled DOGS' livers — vitamin A poisoning killed Mertz (skin peeling off); the Inuit had always known never to eat polar-bear liver. T5: vitamin A is fat-soluble, so cooking carrots in butter/oil unlocks far more of the carotene than eating them dry.
topics.source: Carrot myth / John 'Cat's Eyes' Cunningham / AI radar cover story: Smithsonian Magazine, CEENTA, Atlas Obscura, Explore the Archive (all consulted). Liver toxicity / Mawson & Mertz 1913 Far Eastern Party / Inuit avoidance / de Veer 1597 / husky-liver toxic dose: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypervitaminosis_A and A-Z Animals (consulted). Beta-carotene conversion + self-limiting + fat-soluble absorption: standard nutrition consensus.
topics.framing_note: Invert the wonder — put the propaganda claim / the 'liver that kills' in the stem, make the knowable food-fact the answer; never a definition. KEY RAIL: the carrot claim is HALF-true (restores normal night vision in deficiency, no super-vision) — don't over-debunk into 'carrots do nothing for eyes,' and only ANIMAL retinol overdoses, never plant beta-carotene. Dinner-test payoff = the Mawson/Mertz sled-dog-liver rung.

topics.name: Vitamin C, scurvy & the Royal Navy
topics.strand: Micros: vitamins & where you get them
topics.scope: The hook: a disease that rotted sailors' gums and reopened old wounds on long voyages, cured by ordinary fresh fruit. T1: scurvy strikes when there's no fresh food for months (bleeding gums, loose teeth, wounds that won't heal); the fix is fresh CITRUS (oranges & lemons). T2: the missing thing is vitamin C, needed to build COLLAGEN, the 'glue' holding skin, gums and blood vessels together, so without it the body literally comes apart. T2 (surprise source): a raw red BELL PEPPER carries more vitamin C than an orange (also broccoli, blackcurrants) — citrus isn't the only star. T3: James Lind's 1747 trial aboard HMS Salisbury gave sailors different remedies; only the pair on oranges & lemons recovered — one of the first controlled clinical experiments. T3: the word 'ascorbic acid' literally means 'anti-scurvy' (a-scorbutic). T3: the Navy issued citrus juice from ~1795, earning British sailors the nickname 'limeys.' T4: the Navy later swapped Mediterranean LEMONS for cheaper West Indian LIMES — but limes hold far LESS vitamin C, and boiling the juice and storing it in copper destroyed most of what remained, so scurvy came BACK on polar expeditions. T4: humans (and guinea pigs) are among the rare animals that CAN'T make their own vitamin C — a broken GULO gene — so we must eat it, while a dog's liver makes its own. T5: vitamin C is fragile, wrecked by heat, air, light and time (why long-stored juice failed). T5 (payoff): shelf-stable vitamin C came from FERMENTED food — Captain Cook carried sauerkraut (fermented cabbage keeps its C) to keep crews scurvy-free.
topics.source: Grokipedia/page/Scurvy attempted FIRST but returned HTTP 403 to the fetcher; corroborated via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scurvy (fetched: Lind 1747 HMS Salisbury controlled trial; 1795 Admiralty lemon ration; Napoleonic-era switch to West Indian limes with lower vitamin C, degraded by light/air/copper tubing; 1918 study found Navy lime juice near-zero antiscorbutic power → polar-expedition scurvy; 'limey' origin; GULO pseudogene). Bell-pepper vitamin C content and sauerkraut/Cook: standard nutrition + maritime-history consensus (build stage to pull primary cite).
topics.framing_note: Scene-led (a sailor's mouth falling apart), never 'What is vitamin C?'; every answer is a concrete food/history fact. KEY RAIL: the lime switch BACKFIRED — limes had LESS vitamin C than lemons, do not imply lime was an upgrade; and don't anachronistically credit Lind with 'vitamin C' (isolated only in the 1930s) — he knew citrus worked, not why. Dinner-test payoff = the sauerkraut rung (fermented cabbage as the shelf-stable cure).

topics.name: Vitamin D: sunlight, fatty fish & the rickets story
topics.strand: Micros: vitamins & where you get them
topics.scope: The hook: the one vitamin your own skin manufactures — and the disease that appeared when cities blocked the sun. T1: vitamin D is the 'sunshine vitamin' — your SKIN makes it when sunlight hits it, the one vitamin you don't strictly need from food. T2: in food the best sources are fatty fish (salmon, mackerel, sardines) plus egg yolks; it's rare enough that milk is often fortified with it. T2: the old remedy was cod liver oil — a spoonful of fish-liver oil loaded with vitamin D (and A). T3: too little in childhood causes RICKETS — soft bones that bow under a child's weight into bowed legs, because calcium can't harden bone without vitamin D. T3 (history): rickets exploded in the smoky, sunless industrial cities of 1800s Britain — tall tenements and coal smog kept sunlight off slum children. T4: the skin makes vitamin D from UVB sunlight acting on a cholesterol-like molecule, so darker skin (more melanin) needs more sun and far-north winters make food sources matter more. T4 (payoff): traditional far-north diets beat the no-sun problem with food — the Inuit got vitamin D from fatty fish and marine-mammal fat, not sunlight.
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vitamin_D and NCBI Endotext NBK278935 (7-dehydrocholesterol + UVB 290-320nm synthesis; fatty fish/fish-liver-oil sources). PubMed 30627846 (cod liver oil, UV radiation, eradication of rickets). Rickets in industrial cities + melanin/latitude: consensus across the consulted sources.
topics.framing_note: Scene-led (the sunless slum child, the spoon of cod liver oil), answers are foods or the disease. RAIL: skin makes it from UVB SUNLIGHT specifically (not warmth or visible light); rickets is the childhood bone-softening disease. Mostly settled science (optimal-dose debate exists but core is not contested) so vision_mandated:false. Dinner-test payoff = the Inuit fatty-fish/marine-fat rung (food replacing the missing sun).

topics.name: Vitamin K & the fermented-food payoff
topics.strand: Micros: vitamins & where you get them
topics.scope: The hook: why this vitamin got the letter K, out of alphabetical order. T3: vitamin K is the CLOTTING vitamin — its job is to make blood clot and seal wounds; the 'K' comes from the Danish word Koagulation, named by its discoverer Henrik Dam. T3: the everyday form (K1) comes from leafy greens — kale, spinach, broccoli — the green leaves again. T4 (payoff): a second form, K2, comes from FERMENTED and animal foods — aged cheese, egg yolk, and above all natto, the sticky fermented soybeans of Japan (made by Bacillus subtilis bacteria). T4: K2's emerging role is as a 'traffic cop' for calcium, steering it into bones and teeth and away from clogging arteries — a reason traditional fermented and grass-fed foods are prized.
topics.source: Vitamin K discovery (Henrik Dam, Danish 'koagulation', 1929/1935, 1943 Nobel), K1 phylloquinone in leafy greens, K2 menaquinone in natto/cheese/organ meat (MK-7 from Bacillus subtilis natto): consulted search across dsm-firmenich, boltpharmacy, Oxford Vitality, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vitamin_K. K2→arterial-calcium role: EMERGING science (Rotterdam Study lineage) — flag as emerging, not settled.
topics.framing_note: Invert the wonder — the stem asks why it's 'K' (out of order); answer is the koagulation/clotting fact; never a definition-shell. RAIL: K = koagulation (Danish, Dam); K1 = greens, K2 = fermented/animal; the K2-steers-calcium-from-arteries claim is EMERGING, present it as promising-not-proven. vision_mandated:true (the K2/arterial-calcium traditional-foods claim is contested/emerging). Dinner-test payoff = the natto/fermented-food K2 rung.

topics.name: What cooking does to vitamins: why steaming beats boiling
topics.strand: Micros: vitamins & where you get them
topics.scope: The hook: the vitamins you pour down the drain. T1: cooking can DESTROY vitamins — vitamin C is the fragile one, wrecked by heat and dissolved out into the cooking water. T2: that's why STEAMING or microwaving vegetables keeps more vitamins than BOILING — the veg never soaks in water that carries the vitamins away. T3: the split — WATER-soluble vitamins (C and the B's) leach into cooking water and break down with heat; FAT-soluble ones (A, D, E, K) shrug off heat but can be lost in fat you drain off. T3: the pro move is to keep the vitamin-rich cooking water for soup, gravy or stock (the traditional 'pot liquor') so the leached vitamins aren't wasted. T4 (payoff): cooking isn't all loss — heat breaks down cell walls to RELEASE nutrients raw food locks away: cooked tomatoes yield more usable lycopene, cooked carrots more usable beta-carotene than raw.
topics.source: Water- vs fat-soluble heat/leaching behavior: NCBI NBK234920 and PMC11242131 (fat-soluble stability) plus standard food-science consensus. Heat-released lycopene (cooked tomato) and beta-carotene bioavailability: well-established food-science consensus (Cornell/Rui Hai Liu tomato-lycopene work; USDA retention data) — build stage to attach primary cites; not fabricated but not re-verified live this session.
topics.framing_note: Scene-led (the pot of boiling water stealing the vitamins) and prep-framed (the game action is cooking — 'you steam it / you boil it' voice is fine). RAIL: water-soluble (C, B) leach + degrade with heat; fat-soluble (A,D,E,K) survive heat; and cooking is NOT pure loss — some nutrients (lycopene, beta-carotene) rise with heat.
