Settled → vision_mandated:false. Dinner-test payoff = the T4 rung (cooking can INCREASE available nutrients).

topics.name: Ancestral eating: keto, paleo, carnivore
topics.scope: Low-carb and ancestral diets as schools. T1: what a KETO plate looks like vs a normal one — almost no bread, sugar, or pasta, lots of fat and meat; the defining rule is cutting carbs way down (a kid can identify keto foods). T2 (mechanism): with carbs scarce, the LIVER turns fat into KETONES for the brain and body to burn instead of glucose — 'ketosis,' the engine of the diet. T3 (origin payoff): keto wasn't invented for weight loss — doctors at the Mayo Clinic created it in the 1920s to control severe childhood EPILEPSY seizures, and it's still prescribed for that today. T4: PALEO's premise — eat what a pre-farming hunter-gatherer could (meat, fish, eggs, vegetables, nuts) and skip what farming and industry added (grains, most dairy, refined sugar); the defining exclusion. T5: CARNIVORE, the extreme (animal foods only), raises the real scientific puzzle these diets must answer — where do you get vitamin C and fiber without plants? (fresh and organ meats supply some vitamin C; the fiber question is the honest open debate). Fair answer states the open question, not a verdict.
topics.source: Wikipedia 'Ketogenic diet' (Wilder/Mayo Clinic 1921, ketone bodies, epilepsy use); news-medical and Johns Hopkins Epilepsy Center keto-history timeline; Loren Cordain paleo-diet premise; general low-carb metabolism references
topics.framing_note: FOOD-ANCHORED (what's on the plate; the ketone rung is fat-to-fuel biology, not a bare definition). Steel-man: these help many people with weight and metabolic control AND carry real open questions (micronutrients, long-term data) — no cheerleading and no dismissal. ACCURACY RAIL: keto's 1920s epilepsy origin is real; frame paleo as a MODERN premise, not a claim that 'cavemen ate exactly this.' Payoff = the epilepsy-origin rung (T3).

topics.name: Cholesterol and the egg's comeback
topics.scope: Dietary cholesterol's small effect. T1: the egg's cholesterol lives in the YOLK — and eggs were the food doctors told people to cut for decades (the setup). T2: the old logic — eating high-cholesterol food (eggs, shrimp) was assumed to raise your blood cholesterol nearly one-for-one, the intuitive claim that turned out shaky. T3 (mechanism): your own LIVER makes most of the cholesterol in your body and dials its production DOWN when you eat more, which is why dietary cholesterol moves blood cholesterol far less than expected. T4 (payoff): the reversal — in 2015 the U.S. Dietary Guidelines DROPPED the longstanding cholesterol limit, stating dietary cholesterol is not a 'nutrient of concern for overconsumption'; eggs came back. T5: the honest nuance — cholesterol isn't a toxin at all, it's the raw material your body uses to build cell membranes, vitamin D, and hormones (why you can't live without it).
topics.source: 2015-2020 Dietary Guidelines for Americans and DGAC report ('not a nutrient of concern for overconsumption'; 300mg limit removed); CNN 2015 'Cholesterol in food not a concern' coverage; PMC 'The Fifty Year Rehabilitation of the Egg'; NIH cholesterol physiology references
topics.framing_note: FOOD-ANCHORED (the egg yolk is the anchor). Lean: eggs were wrongly demonized and dietary cholesterol's effect is small — but steel-man that blood LDL still matters for heart health (don't overclaim 'cholesterol doesn't matter'). ACCURACY RAIL: 2015 guidelines dropped the 300mg LIMIT; they did NOT declare cholesterol irrelevant to health. Payoff = the 2015 reversal rung (T4).

topics.name: Gluten, wheat, and the fructan twist
topics.scope: Celiac vs the contested 'gluten sensitivity.' T1 (mechanism): what gluten DOES in the kitchen — it's the stretchy protein network in wheat that traps gas and lets bread rise and dough turn chewy (why you knead), a food fact before any health claim. T2: the real disease — CELIAC disease is a genuine autoimmune reaction in which gluten damages the small intestine, so for these people avoiding gluten is medical necessity, not a fad (the settled anchor). T3: the contested middle — many people without celiac feel better off wheat ('non-celiac gluten sensitivity'), and the debate is whether it's really the gluten or something else (the open question). T4 (payoff): the plot twist from blinded studies — for many self-reported cases the culprit may not be gluten at all but FODMAPs (fructans, a fermentable carb in wheat that ferments in the gut and causes bloating); the suspect gets swapped. T5: the knowable takeaway a cook can use — traditional SOURDOUGH's long fermentation partly breaks down both gluten and fructans, which is why some wheat-sensitive people tolerate it better (a technique-anchored payoff).
topics.source: Skodje et al. 2018 Gastroenterology (fructan, not gluten, triggers symptoms in self-reported NCGS); Biesiekierski & Gibson (Monash Univ.) low-FODMAP work; general references on celiac disease (autoimmune, gliadin/glutenin) vs NCGS vs wheat allergy; sourdough long-fermentation gluten/fructan reduction studies
topics.framing_note: FOOD-ANCHORED (bread, dough, sourdough). Steel-man: celiac is real and serious; NCGS is contested and may be fructans for many — don't mock gluten-free people OR treat NCGS as fully established. ACCURACY RAIL: keep the terms distinct — gluten = the wheat PROTEIN (gliadin/glutenin), fructans = the FODMAP CARB; celiac ≠ NCGS ≠ wheat allergy. Payoff = the fructan-not-gluten rung (T4); sourdough is the cook's-takeaway payoff (T5).

topics.name: Raw milk vs. pasteurized
topics.scope: The genuine both-sides dilemma. T1: what pasteurizing milk actually does — gently HEATS it to kill germs (named for Louis Pasteur); raw milk is milk that skipped that step (the setup). T2: the FDA/CDC case against raw milk — it can carry dangerous bacteria (Listeria, Salmonella, E. coli) that heating would have killed, a real risk especially for young children. T3: the proponents' steel-man — heat also changes milk, denaturing some enzymes and whey proteins and killing the milk's live bacteria, which is exactly what raw-milk drinkers want to keep intact. T4 (payoff): the evidence that keeps the debate alive — large European studies of thousands of farm children found kids who drank FARM/raw milk had notably LESS asthma and allergy; the protective signal is real in the data. T5: the catch that makes it a true dilemma — the SAME researchers warned that raw milk's pathogen risk means they still cannot recommend it, and the protective proteins are heat-sensitive so ordinary pasteurized milk loses them; the fair answer holds BOTH truths.
topics.source: FDA 'The Dangers of Raw Milk'; CDC raw-milk outbreak surveillance (1998-2018 data); Loss et al. 2011 GABRIELA study, J Allergy Clin Immunol (farm/raw milk vs asthma & atopy, ~8,000 children, and the authors' own safety caveat); Wikipedia 'Pasteurization' (Pasteur 1864, HTST)
topics.framing_note: FOOD-ANCHORED (milk and the heating step). This is the MODEL steel-man-both-sides ladder: the allergy-protection signal is REAL and the pathogen risk is REAL. Lean sympathetic to the traditional case but NEVER hide the danger to children. ACCURACY RAIL: don't claim raw milk is proven safe, and don't claim the allergy benefit is disproven — both are supported; present the dilemma honestly. Payoff = the farm-children asthma rung (T4).

topics.name: Red meat and the cancer scare
topics.scope: Nutrition value vs the headline risk. T1: why humans prize red meat nutritionally — it's the richest easy source of complete protein plus iron and B12, nutrients that build blood and are hard to get elsewhere (the empowerment fact: why a kid needs it). T2 (mechanism): the iron in meat is HEME iron, which the gut absorbs far better than the non-heme iron in spinach and plants — why 'eat your spinach for iron' is only half the story. T3: the 2015 headline — the WHO's cancer agency (IARC) classified PROCESSED meat (bacon, hot dogs) as a definite carcinogen and red meat as 'probably,' what the scare was actually about. T4 (payoff, nuance): what that classification really means — it rates the STRENGTH of evidence, not how dangerous a food is; the actual added risk from a daily bacon habit is small, and a 2019 expert panel argued the evidence to cut back on red meat was weak. Fair answer: 'modest risk, contested advice.' T5: the less-contested cooking angle — charring meat black over high heat forms compounds (HCAs and PAHs) linked to cancer risk, so HOW you cook it may matter more than that it's red (a technique fact a cook can use).
topics.source: IARC/WHO 2015 Monograph vol. 114 (processed meat Group 1, red meat Group 2A; 50g/day → ~18% relative colorectal-cancer risk); Johnston et al. 2019 NutriRECS, Annals of Internal Medicine (weak evidence to reduce); NIH/NCI on HCAs and PAHs in charred meat
topics.framing_note: FOOD-ANCHORED (meat, bacon, and how it's cooked). Lean: red meat is nutritionally valuable and the cancer scare was overstated in headlines — but steel-man that processed meat's colorectal-cancer link is genuine, just small in absolute terms. ACCURACY RAIL: Group 1 / 2A rate EVIDENCE STRENGTH, not potency — do NOT equate a bacon rasher with a cigarette. Payoff = the 'classification is not danger-level' rung (T4).

topics.name: Seed oils: the omega-6 and heated-oil debate
topics.scope: The fight over industrial seed oils. T1: seed oils (soybean, canola, corn, sunflower, safflower) are pressed/extracted from tiny SEEDS, unlike olive, avocado, or coconut oil which come from the fruit or flesh — a kid can sort 'seed' oils from 'fruit' oils. T2: how they're made — unlike olive oil (just pressed), industrial seed oils are pulled out with a chemical SOLVENT (hexane) and high heat, then refined, bleached, and deodorized. T3: they're rich in the omega-6 fat LINOLEIC acid, a POLYUNSATURATED fat, and the modern-diet worry is the lopsided omega-6-to-omega-3 RATIO (we eat far more omega-6 than our ancestors). T4 (dinner-test payoff): because polyunsaturated fats have many fragile double bonds, REHEATING or REUSING oil for deep-frying oxidizes them into reactive ALDEHYDES — the strongest, most chemistry-real part of the skeptic case (a fresh-vs-repeatedly-fried-oil fact). T5: the mainstream steel-man — swapping saturated fat for polyunsaturated seed oil reliably LOWERS LDL cholesterol, and large reviews tie higher linoleic acid to LOWER heart-disease risk, which is why bodies like the AHA still recommend them; a fair rung SUMMARIZES the debate, not a verdict.
topics.source: Grokipedia (grokipedia.com/page/Seed_oil — attempted, HTTP 403 to fetch bot); Wikipedia 'Seed oil misinformation' (oil list, hexane/RBD, EPA hexane data, AHA omega-6 advisory, FDA GRAS); AHA Science Advisory on omega-6 (Harris/Sacks); published work on aldehyde (4-HNE) formation in repeatedly heated frying oil (Grootveld, De Montfort Univ)
topics.framing_note: FOOD-ANCHORED: every answer is about an oil, how it's made, or what happens in the pan — never a bare 'omega-6 is inflammatory' slogan. Lean SKEPTICAL of heated/reused oil (the aldehyde rung is real, defensible chemistry) while stating the mainstream LDL/PUFA case honestly; contested rungs' correct answers summarize the debate, distractors caricature ('seed oils are literally poison' / 'omega-6 is always healthy, period'). ACCURACY RAIL: do NOT claim seed oils are proven to cause disease (not established) and do NOT claim trace hexane residue is dangerous (it evaporates). The reheated-oil aldehyde rung (T4) is the dinner-test payoff.

topics.name: Sugar vs. fat: who was the real villain?
topics.scope: How fat took the blame while sugar got a pass. T1: in the mid-1900s a scientist named Ancel Keys convinced the world that dietary FAT caused heart attacks — why low-fat everything took over the table (the historical claim; Keys is context, the tested fact is the food/claim). T2: a British rival, John Yudkin, pointed at SUGAR instead in his 1972 book 'Pure, White and Deadly' — and lost the argument badly at the time. T3 (payoff): decades later, documents surfaced showing that in 1967 the SUGAR industry secretly PAID Harvard scientists to publish a review that blamed fat and downplayed sugar (the food-history reveal). T4: the low-fat era backfired — when makers stripped fat out of foods, they added SUGAR to keep them tasty (the SnackWell's effect), a mechanism a kid can grasp. T5: where it landed — sugar, especially in sugary drinks, is now taken seriously as a driver of obesity and metabolic disease, so Yudkin was partly VINDICATED, though 'sugar is the single cause' overshoots; fair answer summarizes the shift.
topics.source: Wikipedia 'Pure, White and Deadly' and 'John Yudkin' (Keys rivalry, 1972 book, 2012 Lustig reissue/vindication); Kearns, Schmidt & Glantz 2016 JAMA Internal Medicine (Sugar Research Foundation 1967 Harvard/NEJM documents); NPR and PBS NewsHour 2016 coverage; Marion Nestle Food Politics analysis
topics.framing_note: FOOD-ANCHORED — the tested ANSWER is always a food (fat, sugar, the reformulated low-fat product), never a bare person or date; names (Keys, Yudkin, Hegsted) stay as context. Lean: the anti-fat crusade overcorrected and sugar got a pass — but steel-man that Keys wasn't purely wrong and 'sugar is the only villain' is also too simple. ACCURACY RAIL: describe the 1967 episode precisely (industry funded a biased review; the authors' conflict wasn't disclosed) — not 'sugar proven to cause all disease.' Payoff = the sugar-industry-funded-Harvard rung (T3).

topics.name: The salt wars
topics.scope: Is less salt always better? T1: salt isn't optional — sodium is an essential mineral your nerves and muscles can't work without, and it was once so precious it was used as pay (the root of the word 'salary'); the setup that salt is a need, not just a vice. T2: the everyday chemistry a cook knows — table salt is sodium CHLORIDE, and it's the sodium half the health debate is about. T3: the old blanket rule — health agencies told EVERYONE to slash salt because high sodium raises blood pressure in some people (a real effect for salt-sensitive people). T4 (payoff): the twist big studies found — the sodium/heart-risk curve is J-SHAPED: very HIGH salt is risky, but very LOW salt also tracked with higher risk (the body fights back and retains sodium); the fair answer is 'there's a healthy middle,' not 'less is always better.' T5: the cooking payoff — most of the salt people eat doesn't come from the shaker; roughly 70% is already built into processed and restaurant food, so salting your own whole-food cooking is a small slice of the total (a fact a cook can act on).
topics.source: Mente, O'Donnell, Yusuf et al. 2018 PURE analysis, The Lancet (J-shaped sodium/CV-event curve; risk concentrated above ~5g/day); European Salt Action Network scientific statement (the population-reduction rebuttal); CDC/NHANES data on ~70% of sodium from processed/restaurant food; sodium physiology references
topics.framing_note: FOOD-ANCHORED (salt the ingredient and salted foods). Lean skeptical of the 'everyone must go very low' orthodoxy and sympathetic to salting real food — but steel-man that salt reduction genuinely helps salt-sensitive and hypertensive people. ACCURACY RAIL: the J-curve comes from observational data and is contested by some bodies — state it as 'evidence suggests a middle range,' not settled fact. Payoff = the J-curve rung (T4).

topics.name: The saturated-fat reversal
topics.scope: How 'artery-clogging' butter got re-examined. T1: which everyday foods are mostly SATURATED fat and stay solid at room temperature — butter, lard, beef tallow, coconut oil, cheese (sort solid animal/coconut fats from liquid oils). T2: the old advice — for decades official guidance said saturated fat clogs arteries and told people to swap butter for margarine and vegetable oil (the historical claim). T3: WHY they said it — saturated fat raises LDL ('bad') cholesterol in the blood, the diet-heart hypothesis and the part that's still true. T4: the nuance later research added — saturated fat also raises HDL and shifts LDL toward larger, fluffier particles, and the health answer depends on what you REPLACE it with (swapping it for refined carbs/sugar didn't help). T5 (payoff): the 2010s re-examination — large pooled analyses (a 2010 and a 2014 meta-analysis) found the direct link between saturated fat and heart disease was much WEAKER than assumed, so guidelines softened; the fair answer is 'the simple artery-clogging story was overstated,' not 'saturated fat is proven harmless.'
topics.source: Grokipedia (grokipedia.com/page/Saturated_fat — attempted, HTTP 403); Wikipedia 'Saturated fat and cardiovascular disease' (AHA LDL rationale, current WHO/AHA/NHS <10% guidance, food fat percentages); Siri-Tarino et al. 2010 Am J Clin Nutr meta-analysis; Chowdhury et al. 2014 Annals of Internal Medicine meta-analysis; Sacks et al. 2017 AHA Presidential Advisory
topics.framing_note: FOOD-ANCHORED (butter/lard/tallow/coconut/cheese are the anchors). Lean: honest that the old artery-clogging story was oversold, WITHOUT claiming saturated fat is proven protective — steel-man both sides (the LDL rise is real; the hard-outcome link is weak). ACCURACY RAIL: don't say saturated fat 'has no effect on cholesterol' (it does raise LDL) — the contested part is the disease OUTCOME, not the LDL mechanism. Payoff = the meta-analysis reversal rung (T5).

topics.name: Trans fats: the health food that was the poison
topics.scope: The margarine-to-butter reversal. T1: margarine was invented as a cheap butter substitute (1870s France), and for a century it was sold as the HEART-HEALTHY choice over butter (the reversal setup). T2 (origin/mechanism): to turn liquid vegetable oil into a solid, shelf-stable spread, makers bubble HYDROGEN through it — partial HYDROGENATION, the same process that made Crisco shortening in 1911. T3: the catch — partial hydrogenation creates TRANS fats, an unnatural fat shape, and trans fat is the one fat that both RAISES bad LDL and LOWERS good HDL, worse for the heart than the butter it replaced. T4 (payoff): the reversal — evidence in the 1990s pinned trans fat to heart disease, and the U.S. FDA ultimately revoked its safe status and BANNED artificial trans fat from food (phased out by 2018); the 'healthy' margarine turned out to be the villain and butter was largely vindicated. T5: why it was everywhere anyway — partially hydrogenated oil gave fried fast food and packaged baked goods long shelf life and crisp texture, the trade-off that made it so widely used before the ban.
topics.source: FDA 'Final Determination Regarding Partially Hydrogenated Oils' (2015 GRAS revocation; June 2018 compliance); PMC 'The Demise of Artificial Trans Fat: A History of a Public Health Achievement' (margarine 1870, hydrogenation ~1910, Crisco 1911); NEJM 'The Trans-Fat Ban'; Harvard Health trans-fat overview
topics.framing_note: FOOD-ANCHORED (margarine, Crisco, shortening, fried food). This is the traditional-foods vindication story — the lean is fine, but be FAIR to why hydrogenation was adopted (cheap, shelf-stable, replaced lard) rather than moralizing about industry. ACCURACY RAIL: trans-fat harm is SETTLED science (not the contested part); dates are margarine=1870s France, Crisco=1911, U.S. ban fully in force 2018. Payoff = the ban / butter-vindication rung (T4).

topics.name: Ultra-processed foods
topics.scope: Why engineered food overrides fullness. T1: what makes a food 'ultra-processed' vs just cooked — sorting an apple or a home-cooked stew from a neon breakfast cereal or a snack cake full of ingredients you can't pronounce (the recognizable line). T2: the tell — ultra-processed foods contain industrial ingredients you'd never keep in a home kitchen (emulsifiers, protein isolates, artificial flavorings), the NOVA idea of grouping food by degree of PROCESSING rather than by nutrients. T3 (payoff, mechanism): the 2019 NIH experiment — people given an ultra-processed diet ate about 500 MORE calories a day and gained weight, versus the SAME calories and nutrients delivered from whole food; the food itself drove overeating. T4: why — soft, calorie-dense, hyper-palatable texture and flavor are engineered to be eaten fast and to override fullness signals (the mechanism behind the extra calories). T5: the honest limit — 'ultra-processed' lumps soda together with plain whole-grain bread and plain yogurt, so critics call the category too blunt; fair answer is that processing-degree is a useful-but-imperfect guide, not a law.
topics.source: Hall et al. 2019 Cell Metabolism, NIH inpatient randomized controlled trial (~500 kcal/day, matched macros); NOVA classification (Monteiro et al., Univ. of São Paulo); NIH news release on the UPF study
topics.framing_note: FOOD-ANCHORED (real snack foods vs whole foods). Lean traditional/whole-foods (the Hall RCT is strong evidence) but steel-man that NOVA is a blunt category that critics dispute. ACCURACY RAIL: the ~500-calorie result is from ONE well-controlled RCT with matched macros — state it as that, not 'processed food proven to cause all obesity.' Payoff = the NIH 500-calorie rung (T3).

topics.name: What 'organic' really means
topics.scope: The firm claim vs the contested one. T1: what the 'USDA Organic' label actually promises — grown without synthetic pesticides and fertilizers and without GMOs, NOT a promise of more vitamins (given the label, what does it guarantee?). T2 (payoff): the firm finding — organic produce carries FEWER pesticide residues (a large review found roughly 30% lower likelihood of detectable residue), the best-supported reason to buy organic. T3: the contested finding — big reviews (Stanford 2012) found little consistent NUTRITION difference, while others found modestly higher antioxidants and lower cadmium, so 'organic is more nutritious' is genuinely unsettled. T4: the myth-buster — 'organic' does NOT mean pesticide-FREE; organic farmers use approved NATURAL pesticides (like copper and neem oil), which aren't automatically safer than synthetic ones (the fact that surprises people).
topics.source: Smith-Spangler, Bravata et al. 2012 Annals of Internal Medicine (Stanford meta-analysis of 237 studies: ~30% lower pesticide-residue likelihood, little nutrition difference); Barański et al. 2014 British Journal of Nutrition (higher antioxidants, lower cadmium in organic); USDA National Organic Program standards
topics.framing_note: FOOD-ANCHORED (produce and the label). Steel-man both sides: pesticide-reduction is firm; the nutrition boost is contested; organic still uses (natural) pesticides. Keep the lean MODEST — don't cheerlead OR dismiss organic. ACCURACY RAIL: don't claim organic is proven more nutritious (not established) and don't claim it is pesticide-FREE (false). Payoff = the fewer-residues rung (T2); the natural-pesticide rung (T4) is the surprise.

topics.name: Whole food vs. the pill
topics.scope: Why an isolated nutrient isn't the food. T1: the intuition — if the beta-carotene in carrots is good for you, a beta-carotene PILL should be even better (the setup that turns out wrong). T2: the everyday version — a multivitamin promises the 'good parts' of fruit and veg in one tablet (the claim to test). T3 (payoff): the famous surprise — large 1990s trials gave smokers high-dose beta-carotene SUPPLEMENTS to prevent lung cancer, and the pills INCREASED lung cancer instead; the isolated nutrient behaved opposite to the food. T4 (mechanism): why — in whole food a nutrient arrives packaged with hundreds of others (the 'food matrix'), so pulling one out at megadose can throw the system off; the carrot is not the pill. T5: the honest limit — supplements DO work when you have a genuine deficiency (vitamin D in winter, B12 for vegans, folate in pregnancy, vitamin C for scurvy); the fair answer is 'food first, pills to fix a real gap,' not 'all supplements are useless.'
topics.source: ATBC Study Group 1994 NEJM (alpha-tocopherol/beta-carotene trial, ~18% excess lung cancer in beta-carotene arm) and Omenn et al. 1996 CARET, NEJM (~28% more lung cancer cases); reviews on the food matrix vs isolated-nutrient supplementation; established deficiency-correction uses (D, B12, folate, C)
topics.framing_note: FOOD-ANCHORED (carrots vs the pill; the food matrix). Lean whole-foods ('eat the food, not the extract') but steel-man that TARGETED supplements fix real deficiencies — don't slide into anti-supplement absolutism. ACCURACY RAIL: the beta-carotene/lung-cancer harm was specifically in SMOKERS at high dose — do NOT generalize to 'vitamins cause cancer.' Payoff = the beta-carotene-smoker-trial rung (T3).

strands.strand: Whole vs processed, and your gut

topics.name: Are seed oils bad? The honest fat debate
topics.strand: Whole vs processed, and your gut
topics.scope: A genuine, unsettled nutrition argument, steel-manned both ways. T1: 'seed oils' (soybean, corn, canola, sunflower) are pressed from tiny seeds — you can't squeeze oil from a seed by hand, so these are recent INDUSTRIAL foods, unlike olive oil or butter that people have pressed and churned for millennia. T2: how they're made — seeds are crushed and washed with a petroleum solvent (hexane) to extract every drop, then refined, bleached, and deodorized; critics point to this heavy industrial processing. T3: they're rich in omega-6 linoleic acid, and the critics' case is that the modern diet's omega-6-to-omega-3 ratio ballooned (roughly 1:1 in ancestral diets to about 20:1 today), possibly tilting the body toward inflammation. T4: the steel-man for the mainstream — controlled trials find that replacing saturated fat with linoleic acid LOWERS blood cholesterol and heart-disease risk, so major heart associations still recommend them. T5: the honest verdict — genuinely unsettled; the firmest shared ground is that seed oils are worst as the backbone of deep-FRIED ultra-processed food, while traditional fats (butter, olive oil, tallow) are safe, time-tested choices.
topics.source: Massachusetts General Hospital 'Seed oils: facts & myths'; JACC analysis (linoleic acid replacing saturated fat lowers CVD risk); British Heart Foundation seed-oils explainer; hexane vs cold-press extraction (PMC comparative study); Grokipedia attempted first, unreachable.
topics.framing_note: Scene-led (a bottle of oil, a deep-fryer). Food-anchored answers about the oil, its source, or its making. ACCURACY RAIL: STEEL-MAN BOTH SIDES — never call seed oils 'poison' and never dismiss the critics; present the omega-6 hypothesis AND the trial evidence as competing live positions. Keep the pre-industrial/industrial contrast accurate (olive oil & butter are ancient; seed oils need machinery). Dinner-test payoff = T2 (seed oils are washed out of seeds with a solvent, hexane).

topics.name: Cheese: milk that keeps for years
topics.strand: Whole vs processed, and your gut
topics.scope: Preservation by curdling. T1: cheese is a way to PRESERVE milk — fresh milk spoils in days, but concentrated into cheese it keeps for months or years. T2: the discovery legend — milk carried in a pouch made from a young animal's stomach curdled on the journey into curds and whey, the stomach's enzyme doing the work by accident. T3: the mechanism — rennet (the enzyme chymosin, from a calf's stomach) makes milk's casein proteins clump into solid curds while the watery whey drains off; the more water you press out, the longer the cheese keeps. T4: aging is a controlled ferment — specific microbes ripen the flavor and edible molds are invited on purpose (the blue veins of blue cheese are a deliberately grown mold).
topics.source: Wikipedia 'Rennet' (chymosin from calf abomasum / fourth stomach; use since ~6000 BC; saddlebag-origin legend); cheese aging and Penicillium in blue cheese — standard food science; Grokipedia attempted first, unreachable.
topics.framing_note: Prep-frame fine (you curdle, drain, press, age it), matter-of-fact about the calf-stomach enzyme — not gory. Scene-led, food-anchored answers. ACCURACY RAIL: rennet = chymosin from a calf's fourth stomach; tell the saddlebag-origin as LEGEND, not documented history. Dinner-test payoff = T2/T3 (a stomach enzyme curdles milk — the accidental-saddlebag origin that turned spoilage into cheese).

topics.name: Eat food, mostly plants: the whole-food idea
topics.strand: Whole vs processed, and your gut
topics.scope: The eating philosophy behind the whole strand. T1: Michael Pollan's entire rule fits in seven words — 'Eat food. Not too much. Mostly plants.' — and the trick is what he means by 'food'. T2: by 'food' he means what your great-grandmother would recognize as food, not the engineered 'edible foodlike substances' that wear health claims on the box (his tell: the louder the health claim, the more suspicious you should be). T3: 'nutritionism' names the error of judging a food by its listed nutrients (fat-free! added vitamins!) instead of the whole food — a real food is more than the sum of the numbers on its label. T4: the food-matrix proof — a whole orange and a glass of orange juice carry the same sugar, but the orange's intact fiber and cell walls slow that sugar and fill you up while the juice floods in fast: same nutrients, different food.
topics.source: Michael Pollan, 'In Defense of Food: An Eater's Manifesto' (2008) and michaelpollan.com; Wikipedia 'In Defense of Food' (nutritionism; 'edible foodlike substances'); whole-fruit vs juice glycemic/food-matrix (news-medical.net, PMC); Grokipedia attempted first, unreachable.
topics.framing_note: Scene-led. Verbatim quote allowed for the seven-word rule (a famous slogan, not a Socratic-attribution trap). Food-anchored answers. ACCURACY RAIL: present 'nutritionism' as Pollan's FRAMEWORK/critique, not a proven mechanism; keep the orange-vs-juice payoff HERE and out of the fiber ladder to avoid duplication. LEAN whole-foods but empowerment, not moralizing. Dinner-test payoff = T4 (whole orange vs. its juice — identical sugar, different food).

topics.name: Fiber: the food you can't digest
topics.strand: Whole vs processed, and your gut
topics.scope: Why the indigestible part of plants matters most. T1: fiber is the part of plants your body cannot break down — it passes through largely intact, and that's the point; it lives in beans, oats, vegetables, and fruit skins. T2: two kinds do two jobs — soluble fiber dissolves into a gel that slows digestion (oats, beans), insoluble fiber stays intact and adds bulk that keeps things moving (wheat bran). T3: fiber isn't fuel for YOU — it's fuel for your gut bacteria, which ferment it in the colon (this is exactly what 'prebiotic' means). T4: when bacteria ferment fiber they release short-chain fatty acids, and one of them becomes the MAIN fuel for the cells lining your colon — so fiber feeds your gut wall through a bacterial middleman. T5: a wonder twist — cook a potato or rice, then COOL it, and some starch re-crystallizes into 'resistant starch' your body can't digest but your bacteria love, so cold potato salad feeds your gut more than hot fries from the same potato.
topics.source: Wikipedia 'Short-chain fatty acid' (butyrate = main colonocyte energy source); Wikipedia 'Dietary fiber' (soluble vs insoluble); resistant-starch type-3 (retrogradation on cooling) — standard food science; whole-fruit vs juice glycemic (MDPI/PMC); Grokipedia attempted first, unreachable.
topics.framing_note: Scene-led; invert the wonder — 'the food you can't digest is the point'. Food-anchored answers. ACCURACY RAIL: the tested T4 answer is the CONCEPT (bacteria ferment fiber into fuel for the gut lining), with 'butyrate' as the named payoff/context only — do NOT make the molecule name or a percentage the tested answer (banned minutiae). Dinner-test payoff = T5 (cooled-then-eaten potato/rice makes resistant starch — a genuinely surprising, true, food-anchored fact).

topics.name: Live bugs vs. their food: probiotics and prebiotics
topics.strand: Whole vs processed, and your gut
topics.scope: The two halves of feeding your gut, constantly confused. T1: a 'probiotic' is LIVE beneficial microbes you actually eat — the living cultures in yogurt, kefir, and unpasteurized sauerkraut. T2: heat kills them — pasteurized sauerkraut, cultures baked into bread, or a boiled kombucha are dead, which is why the label brags 'live and active cultures' when they survived. T3: a 'prebiotic' is the opposite job — not a live microbe but the FIBER that feeds the microbes already living in you (inulin in onions, garlic, and chicory; resistant starch in beans and oats). T4: the combo that actually works — eat probiotics to seed the garden AND prebiotics to fertilize it; a bowl of live yogurt with oats and banana does both at once.
topics.source: Wikipedia 'Prebiotic (nutrition)' (definition; inulin/chicory, resistant starch sources); probiotic live-culture basics; Grokipedia attempted first, unreachable.
topics.framing_note: Scene-led, food-anchored — every answer names a real food or what it does. ACCURACY RAIL: keep the probiotic/prebiotic distinction exact (live organisms vs. fiber that feeds them) — that contrast IS the topic, so no blurring. Dinner-test payoff = T2 (cooked/pasteurized sauerkraut has DEAD cultures — a counter-intuitive kitchen fact). Anchor prebiotic examples on specific foods (onion/garlic/chicory) to stay distinct from the fiber ladder.

topics.name: Not every long word is scary: reading a label honestly
topics.strand: Whole vs processed, and your gut
topics.scope: The practical companion to 'ultra-processed', with the chemophobia trap defused. T1 (entry, pitched at T2 difficulty): the working heuristic — the shorter the ingredient list and the more items you can picture as real food, the closer to whole; a scroll of unpronounceable names flags ultra-processing. T2: the catch that keeps you honest — not every chemical-sounding word is bad: 'ascorbic acid' is just vitamin C added to stop spoilage, 'tocopherol' is vitamin E — a scary-looking label can be harmless. T3: the additives actually worth knowing — emulsifiers like polysorbate 80 and carboxymethylcellulose keep oil and water blended in processed food, and early research (mostly in mice, plus a few small human trials) suggests some may thin the gut's protective mucus layer; honest caveat — not proven harmful in people at normal amounts.
topics.source: Chassaing et al. emulsifier research (Nature 2015; PMC controlled-feeding CMC trial) — mucus-layer/microbiome effects, mostly murine plus small human studies; ascorbic acid/tocopherol as vitamin C/E antioxidant additives (standard food science); Grokipedia attempted first, unreachable.
topics.framing_note: Scene-led — a real ingredient list. Food-anchored answers. ACCURACY RAIL: the emulsifier-gut link is EARLY and mostly mouse-based — state it explicitly as a hypothesis, never as established human harm (the honest-evidence discipline). Anti-chemophobia is the point: teach discernment, not fear. Dinner-test payoff = T2 (ascorbic acid on a label is just added vitamin C — a scary word that's benign).

topics.name: Rot you actually want: fermentation across the world
topics.strand: Whole vs processed, and your gut
topics.scope: How the RIGHT microbes preserve and transform food. T1: before refrigeration, people preserved food by inviting the right microbes to take over before rot could — salt, cabbage, and time make sauerkraut that keeps for months. T2: the mechanism — lactic-acid bacteria eat the food's sugars and excrete lactic acid, souring it until it's too acidic for spoilage microbes to survive (kimchi, sauerkraut, sour pickles): sour equals safe. T3: milk ferments too — bacteria convert milk sugar (lactose) into acid that thickens and sours it into yogurt, which is why many lactose-intolerant people tolerate yogurt: the microbes already ate the lactose. T4: some ferments recruit MOLD, not just bacteria — koji mold grown on soybeans and rice starts miso, soy sauce, and sake, its enzymes breaking proteins down into savory glutamate (that's where umami comes from). T5: kombucha ferments with a SCOBY — a rubbery symbiotic mat of bacteria AND yeast together: the yeast makes fizz and a trace of alcohol, the bacteria turn that into tangy acid — a whole tiny ecosystem in a jar.
topics.source: Wikipedia 'Fermentation in food processing' (lacto-fermentation; koji = Aspergillus oryzae for miso/soy sauce/sake; kombucha SCOBY; 13,000-year-old beer residue); yogurt lactose reduction — standard food science; Grokipedia attempted first, unreachable.
topics.framing_note: Prep-frame is fine (you salt/pack/ferment it). Scene-led, food-anchored answers about the food and its microbe-mechanism, never a bare species name as the tested answer. ACCURACY RAIL: kimchi's red chili is POST-Columbian (chili reached Korea ~17th c.; earlier kimchi was chili-free) — never imply ancient chili kimchi. Dinner-test payoff = T4 (soy sauce and miso are made by MOLD grown on soybeans — most kids never guess this).

topics.name: Sauerkraut vs. the sea: fermented cabbage and scurvy
topics.strand: Whole vs processed, and your gut
topics.scope: A food that won sea battles by preventing a disease. T1: scurvy — the sailor's plague — comes from missing ONE nutrient, vitamin C; gums bleed, teeth loosen, old wounds reopen, all from months of salt-meat and hardtack with no fresh produce. T2: James Lind's 1747 shipboard trial — one of history's first controlled experiments — showed citrus (oranges and lemons) cured it, later making British sailors 'limeys', though nobody yet knew the nutrient itself. T3: Captain Cook's edge — he loaded tons of SAUERKRAUT, because fermented cabbage keeps for months at sea and holds its vitamin C (fermentation can even raise it), so his crews stayed scurvy-free without fresh fruit. T4: the getting-them-to-eat-it trick — Cook served kraut only to the officers first so the wary crew would envy it and demand a ration; a psychology move, not an order.
topics.source: Modern Farmer 'How Sauerkraut Helped Save the Age of Sail'; British Library Untold Lives 'Sauerkraut... on Cook's Resolution'; James Lind 1747 citrus trial; scurvy = vitamin C deficiency (settled); Grokipedia attempted first, unreachable.
topics.framing_note: Scene-led — open on the disease/the voyage, food as the hero. Food-anchored answers (the cabbage, the citrus). ACCURACY RAIL: scurvy = vitamin C is SETTLED; frame Lind as EMPIRICAL — vitamin C itself wasn't isolated until the 1930s, so never say Lind or Cook 'knew about vitamin C'. Dinner-test payoff = T3 (fermented cabbage as portable, months-long vitamin C at sea).

topics.name: The 56 disguises of sugar
topics.strand: Whole vs processed, and your gut
topics.scope: Added sugar and how it hides. T1: 'added sugar' is sugar a cook or factory put IN, different from the sugar built into whole fruit or milk — a soda is pure added sugar; an apple's sugar comes wrapped in fiber and water. T2: on an ingredient list sugar hides under dozens of names — dextrose, maltose, cane juice, corn syrup, agave, molasses (the '-ose' ending is usually a tell) — and splitting it across several names keeps any one 'sugar' from topping the list. T3: high-fructose corn syrup is cornstarch broken into glucose, then part-converted to fructose so it's as sweet as table sugar but cheaper and pourable — which is why it fills nearly every sweetened American drink. T4: the WHO says keep 'free sugars' under 10% of daily calories, ideally under 5% (about six teaspoons) — and one can of soda can blow the whole day's budget at once. T5: the honest debate — sugar clearly drives tooth decay and easy excess calories, but whether it's uniquely toxic or just 'empty calories' is argued; the safe reading is that it's a treat, not a food group.
topics.source: WHO 2015 guideline 'Sugars intake for adults and children' (<10%, ideally <5% / ~6 tsp free sugars); UCSF SugarScience & Healthline (56-61 names for sugar); HFCS-55 composition; Grokipedia attempted first, unreachable.
topics.framing_note: Scene-led — open on a label or a soda, never 'What is added sugar?'. Invert the wonder: the WHO percentage and 'six teaspoons' live in the STEM as the hook; the tested answer is the concept/food, never the exact number (banned minutiae). ACCURACY RAIL: distinguish added/free sugar from naturally-occurring sugar in whole fruit correctly. LEAN skeptical of hidden added sugar but do NOT strawman the mainstream (sugar isn't poison). Dinner-test payoff = T2 (sugar's many aliases and the '-ose' tell).

topics.name: The chemistry-set label: what 'ultra-processed' means
topics.strand: Whole vs processed, and your gut
topics.scope: The NOVA idea that sorts food by how much it's been PROCESSED, not by fat/sugar/salt. T1: the practical heuristic a kid can use first — the more ingredients you can't picture as a real thing, the further from whole food (an apple has one ingredient; a snack cake has thirty). T2: Brazilian researcher Carlos Monteiro's NOVA scale ranks by processing — group 1 is whole/minimally-processed food, group 4 is 'ultra-processed', industrially assembled from refined ingredients rather than cooked from recognizable food. T3: the marker ingredients that flag group 4 — high-fructose corn syrup, hydrolysed protein, modified starch, emulsifiers: substances you'd never keep in a home kitchen. T4: the honest evidence — large observational studies link ultra-processed-heavy diets to obesity and heart disease, but correlation can't yet prove the PROCESSING is the culprit versus sheer energy density or crowding out whole foods. T5: Kevin Hall's 2019 NIH controlled-feeding study — people on an ultra-processed diet ate about 500 more calories a day and gained weight versus a whole-food diet matched for sugar, fat, salt and fiber — the first controlled hint that processing itself drives overeating (still one study; mechanism debated).
topics.source: Wikipedia 'Ultra-processed food' (NOVA classification; Carlos Monteiro, Univ. of Sao Paulo 2009; Kevin Hall NIH 2019 controlled-feeding trial); Grokipedia 'Ultra-processed_food' attempted first per source priority but unreachable (HTTP 403 / browser extension offline).
topics.framing_note: Scene-led, never 'What is NOVA?' — open T1 on reading a real ingredient list. Food-anchored answers only: the tested thing is the food/ingredient/finding, never the researcher's name or a bare number. ACCURACY RAIL: NOVA classifies by PROCESSING, not nutrients, and the health link is CORRELATION — do NOT state ultra-processed food as a proven cause; steel-man that it may be energy density or displacement of whole foods. Dinner-test payoff = T5 (the Hall study — same nutrients, more calories eaten; the 500-calorie figure lives in the stem, the concept is the answer).

topics.name: The zoo in your gut: the microbiome
topics.strand: Whole vs processed, and your gut
topics.scope: Your gut as a living ecosystem you feed three times a day. T1: your large intestine houses trillions of bacteria — roughly as many microbial cells as your own body cells — and they help finish digesting your food. T2: a DIVERSE mix of species is the healthy state (like a rainforest, not a lawn), and you build that diversity by eating a variety of plants and fibers. T3: these microbes live on what YOU can't digest — the fiber that reaches the colon is literally their dinner (your leftovers). T4: different foods feed different microbes, which is why 'eat many different plants' beats 'eat a lot of one healthy food' for gut variety. T5: the gut-brain link — gut microbes help make and regulate signaling chemicals (most of the body's serotonin is produced in the gut), so what you feed your microbes can nudge mood and appetite (mechanism still being mapped).
topics.source: Wikipedia 'Gut microbiota'; Wikipedia 'Short-chain fatty acid'; Sender/Fuchs/Milo 2016 (~1:1 microbe-to-human-cell revised estimate); Grokipedia 'Gut_microbiota' attempted first but unreachable (403).
topics.framing_note: Scene-led — open on the living crowd inside, never 'What is the microbiome?'. Food-anchored: every answer ties to what you eat and what the microbes do with it. ACCURACY RAIL: use the current ~1:1 microbe-to-human-cell figure, NOT the outdated 10:1; state the gut-brain link as an active, incompletely-mapped area, not settled cause-and-effect. Dinner-test payoff = T5 (most of your serotonin is made in your gut), framed around food. Keep distinct from the fiber ladder — this is the ecosystem, that is the mechanism.

topics.name: Whole grain vs. white: what milling throws away
topics.strand: Whole vs processed, and your gut
topics.scope: The anatomy of a grain and what refining removes. T1: a wheat kernel has three parts — the bran (fibrous outer coat), the germ (the seed's living embryo, rich in oils and nutrients), and the endosperm (the big starchy middle). T2: white flour is the endosperm ONLY — millers strip out the bran and germ, chiefly because the germ's oils turn rancid fast, so removing them lets flour keep on a shelf for years. T3: what goes out with them — nearly all the grain's fiber and most of its vitamin E and B vitamins live in the discarded bran and germ. T4: 'enriched' flour adds a few B vitamins and iron back by law, but NOT the fiber — so enriched white bread is genuinely not the nutritional equal of whole grain.
topics.source: Wikipedia 'Refined grains'; Harvard T.H. Chan Nutrition Source 'Whole Grains' (bran/germ/endosperm; enrichment adds vitamins not fiber); Grokipedia attempted first, unreachable.
topics.framing_note: Scene-led — open on the kernel or the flour mill, never 'What is refined grain?'. Food-anchored answers. ACCURACY RAIL: enrichment adds back some vitamins and iron but NOT fiber — state this precisely; this is settled food science, so keep the lean gentle. Dinner-test payoff = T2 (white flour is just the endosperm; the nutritious germ is removed for shelf life).
